    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Recent findings suggest that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Industry observers note that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.”.

    In a recent development, RELATED ARTICLEWe know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus?Joshua BentonMarch 25, 2020When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid.

    Industry observers note that for a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously.

    According to recent reports, at the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them.

    Industry observers note that revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026.

    The Online News Association said on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five staffers.

    According to recent reports, “Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Niketa Patel wrote. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.”.

    According to recent reports, LION Publishers noted in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added.

    LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program. But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.”.

    “Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson said.

    OpenNews said in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode”1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON, is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews, told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.”.

    Sources indicate that the three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism remarked Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote.

    According to recent reports, journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he stated. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” a play on Emergency Mode for News, its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [↩].

    According to recent reports, RELATED ARTICLEThis citizen-run organization is teaching thousands of Indonesians to fact-checkHanaa' TameezApril 12, 2023The bill does not distinguish between aggregation and republication. Tech platforms would have to pay even when they surface news link previews or story snippets in their products, including AI search products. The law would also force platforms to compensate publishers when their journalism is used to train AI models.

    Any compensation would be paid through a state-run management organization, which would then distribute the funds to publishers. Platforms that don’t comply could face sanctions, including the loss of their local business permits.

    Social media and search engine companies have come out in force against the bill, with Google leading the campaign.

    Recent findings suggest that indonesia is a massive market for global digital platforms with roughly 230 million internet people. In 2023, Indonesia had the fifth-most Google users of any country in the world, with traffic reaching 4.42 billion searches.

    RELATED ARTICLEMeta will remove legit news from Facebook and Instagram in Canada — but may leave the bad stuff upLaura Hazard OwenAugust 2, 2023As of October 2026, 92% of internet users in Indonesia reported using WhatsApp, with Instagram and Facebook falling close behind at 84% and 79% respectively, according to We Are Social’s Digital 2027 report.

    On Wednesday, a Google official argued that the bill would limit access to news, according to Reuters.

    Berni Moestafa, Meta’s head of public policy in Indonesia, testified that if the bill is passed “publishers could lose readership traffic as well as potential advertising and subscription revenue.”.

    Back in 2023, Canada passed the Online News Act, its own, albeit narrower law which required platforms like Google and Meta to pay publishers for sharing or linking to their content. Meta responded by blocking news links on Facebook and Instagram in Canada altogether.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale. Trusted by over 700 organizations worldwide, including 9 of top 10 US banks, Camunda helps enterprises boost operational efficiency, accelerate time-to-value, and deliver better customer experiences.Fully remote and global, we are in the middle of something bigger: transforming into an AI-first organisation, built on our own platform. Visionary in 2025 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies. ranked 3rd in Flexa's 2026 Most Flexible Companies, We’re growing fast and looking for top talent to join our team. If you want meaningful work, visible impact and put something genuinely rare on your CV, keep reading.

    Hi there! We're hiring an Information Security Engineer with a focus on Application Security to join our Information Security team at Camunda.

    We are a team that takes security seriously without making it feel like a locked door. We work in a transparent, straightforward way, and we care about doing the work right rather than just checking a compliance box.

    Sources indicate that you will work side by side with our R&D engineers: reviewing designs, threat modeling latest features, digging into code and helping teams make good, risk-based decisions about the vulnerabilities that come in. You'll also help build the internal tools that make this work scale, including our CVE registry and the LLM-assisted workflows we use to analyse code and triage findings.

    Sources indicate that camunda is an AI-first tech giant, and InfoSec is no exception: AI agents are part of how we review code, assess vulnerabilities, and build our tools. You will help shape how that works.

    Sources indicate that this is a hands-on role for someone who already has solid AppSec foundations and wants to grow. We are a generalist team, so you will also take part in our on-call rotation and incident response, and get exposure to other areas of security. But most of your time will be spent with engineers and building and maintaining internal tools and processes.

    Vulnerability management: triage findings from SCA, container and code scanning, external reports and internal security testing; assess whether Camunda is actually affected; agree fix / mitigate / accept with engineering and follow through to release.

    Threat modeling and security reviews: run threat modeling sessions and design reviews with R&D teams for newly introduced features and architecture changes, and turn the results into concrete, prioritised actions.

    Code analysis with LLMs: use and improve LLM-assisted tooling (agents, prompts, reusable skills) to review code, validate findings and reproduce issues, while applying your own judgement to know when the model is wrong.

    Industry observers note that build internal security tooling: contribute to the CVE registry and related automation that connects scanners, engineering teams, and customer communication. Much of it is built on Camunda itself.

    Help engineers do the secure thing by default: answer questions, review pull requests, improve guidelines and occasionally run a session or workshop.

    On-call and incident response: share the InfoSec on-call rotation with the other engineers and help investigate and resolve security incidents.

    Support the wider team: help write security advisories for our customers, answer customer security questions and support audits.

    What You Will Bring to the Role.

    Around 3+ years in security or software engineering, with at least 2 of them working on application or product security (AppSec, product security, pentesting, or a security-focused developer role all count).

    Experience at a SaaS or software product organization, working closely with engineering teams that ship often through modern CI/CD and cloud environments.

    Hands-on vulnerability triage: you've worked with tools like Snyk, Trivy, Semgrep, CodeQL or similar, can tell a real issue from a false positive, and can explain how exploitable something actually is in context (CVSS, exploitability, configuration).

    Recent findings suggest that threat modeling and design review experience (e.g. STRIDE) on real systems, ideally web apps, APIs, or distributed services.

    Industry observers note that you read and write code. You're comfortable reading Java (Camunda is built on it) well enough to follow a data flow and spot a security bug. You can write scripts and small tools and contribute to an existing codebase with review.

    You build with AI, not just chat with it. You use AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot or similar) in your daily work to write tools, analyse code or automate tasks. And you know their output still needs a second look, especially when it comes to security.

    Clear, friendly communication with engineers. You see yourself as an enabler, not a gatekeeper, and you can explain risk to people who aren't security specialists.

    Some Python and/or JavaScript experience, or experience building internal tools.

    Willingness to learn and use Camunda, since we build a lot of our own security automation on it. Prior BPMN / workflow experience is a plus.

    Experience responding to security incidents or being part of an on-call rotation.

    Exposure to security advisories, CVE disclosure or bug bounty programmes.

    Knowledge of AI/LLM security risks (OWASP Top 10 for LLMs / agentic apps, prompt injection, tool abuse).

    Experience securing Kubernetes or container-based workloads, or open-source / B2B software.

    This role is an existing vacancy.

    We offer competitive, fair, and transparent compensation. Salary ranges are location-based, with Standard and Major markets (global tech hubs) reflecting local competition.

    United Kingdom: £75,300.00 to £123,800.00.

    Singapore: S$148,900.00 to S$223,300.00.

    If you’re based elsewhere, you’ll be hired via Remote.com (our global employer partner), and your Talent Acquisition Partner will provide a personalized Total Rewards Calculator after your first interview.

    Equity: We also offer equity (where applicable) through our Virtual Stock Option Plan (VSOP).

    According to recent reports, we invest in your wellbeing, growth, and ability to connect, along with perks that support you no matter where you’re based. Our benefits are globally designed and locally delivered where applicable.

    Remote & Flexible: Work from anywhere with the setup that suits you, home office budget, co-working space support, and flexible time off to recharge when you need it.

    In Person Connection: We invest in meaningful face time through our Annual Kickoff (Vienna in 2025, Madrid in 2026!), team offsites, and Camundi Connection Budgets, including contributing to meetups while travelling,, and local gatherings with fellow Camundi.

    Health & Wellbeing: Access locally tailored healthcare, Modern Health for global mental wellbeing, and our Live Well Lifestyle Spending Account (LSA), a flexible, global benefit that puts you in control of your whole life, not just work, from: staying active, to caring for family, exploring personal passions, meaningful experiences, and investing in your financial wellbeing. The Live Well program rolls out in 2026 and scales to €1,000 annually from 2027.

    Financial Security: Retirement and pension plans (often with organization contributions), plus life and disability insurance where relevant.

    Professional Growth: Up to $/€/£1,000 per year for self-driven learning: courses, certifications, books, you decide!

    #8185. WordPress 7.2 Arrives Dec. 8 – Last-Minute Changes Still Being Made via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2670 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    WordPress 7.2 Arrives Dec. 8 – Last-Minute Changes Still Being Made via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This version has, in beta, turned on a newly introduced public address on updated sites.
    • Switching it off will require coding, as there are no settings available via the WordPress dashboard to disable this feature.
    • That makes /random/ the 7.2 change most sites will need to decide on before updating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    WordPress 7.2 is due on Dec. 8. This version has, in beta, turned on a newly introduced public address on updated sites. /random/ directs you to a random published post. Versions of the address also do this within categories, tags, author archives, or eligible custom post types.

    This feature is on by default. Switching it off will require coding, as there are no settings available via the WordPress dashboard to disable this feature. Further, in the November roundup of the WordPress Developer Blog, the filter name listed doesn’t match the actual filter name used in the code. Copying the name from the Developer Blog will have no effect.

    That makes /random/ the 7.2 change most sites will need to decide on before updating. The new Secrets API, a way for plugins to store credentials, was removed from 7.2 on Nov. 17. That came days after Matt Mullenweg, who leads the release, sided with a request to pull it.

    Core’s fresh AI pieces are tools for developers and plugins, and none of them adds an AI feature visitors or editors will see.

    In a recent development, beta five is the latest test release, and WordPress notes not to run it on production sites. The first release candidate (RC1) is due Nov. 17, so details can still change before the final release.

    Recent findings suggest that aaron Jorbin’s developer note opens, “A request to example.com/random/ will lead end customers to a randomly selected published post. The feature is on by default.”.

    The /random/ path and its category, tag, author, and post type versions use the default base with pretty permalinks. The base is translatable, and a new field on the Permalinks screen changes it. The development code also responds to a random query variable, so ?random works too on the home page and archives. Since a Nov. 16 change, a search URL that includes it redirects to the same search without the parameter.

    Recent findings suggest that by default, posts are eligible. Pages and attachments aren’t. Custom post types are considered eligible if they’re publicly queryable, have archives and the developer hasn’t registered them with 'randomable' => false. The code filters for only published posts (with no password).

    Industry observers note that it uses a 302 redirect. The development code sends no-cache headers and includes the header X-Robots-Tag: noindex, follow with the 302 redirect response. This header covers the original /random/ request, but not the post this redirects to. If there is no match to the query, the request will return a 404.

    Recent findings suggest that if you’ve created a published page with the slug “random,” then this will override the redirect. The same thing happens if you create a post with the slug “random,” when permalinks are set to use the post name. Peter Wilson confirmed this in the comments after Daniel Iser raised it, and recommended using a base like “shuffle” instead.

    Random queries run from the main WP_Query, so pre_get_posts callbacks that change archives will also affect their random redirect. Developers wishing to target random requests only should use wp_is_random_content_query().

    Industry observers note that turning this feature off is done by adding the one-line mu-plugin shown in the note, add_filter( 'wp_enable_random_content_redirect', '__return_false' );. This will prevent WordPress from generating rewrite rules for random content, hide the base field on the Permalinks screen, and ignore the query variable. The code’s documentation says that flushing the rewrite rules is necessary after changing the filter value.

    The roundup’s version, wp_enable_random_content_direct, isn’t used anywhere in the code.

    Random redirects made their initial appearance in the code on Sept. 21; at this point they were an optional ?random query that needed sites to return true for a filter called enable_random_content_redirect if they wanted them to be active.

    They were reverted two days after that. The commit message noted of the feature, “The feature is intended to land in WordPress 7.2 but will need some work.”.

    It has been revealed that on Oct. 16, they returned as /random/ rewrite rules turned on, with the filter name changed and the default for the filter set to true. They were added to Beta 1 on Oct. 20.

    Jorbin’s post drew a long thread of objections. Joost de Valk wrote, “This is a horrible idea to turn on by default.” In a later reply, he added, “Now I fear people will randomly end up on invoices, offers, client specific pages, etc.” Responding to another commenter, Jorbin wrote, “The WordPress Philosophies mean that opt-out options are not added for every feature, otherwise the options pages would become unusable.”.

    Mullenweg replied to a commenter whose site already has a page named “random,” writing, “I agree it should not use page URL structure.” In a separate comment, he wrote, “I don’t think this should be an appended pretty URL; the request was just for /?random, just at root.” He also addressed concerns about performance and exposure, saying query strings, searches, and REST calls offer “far more ways” to exhaust a site’s resources.

    As of Nov. 17, no one maintaining the feature had posted a change to its default or its URL structure. Since the note, code changes from Nov. 12 to Nov. 17 have adjusted when the redirect fires, how it treats searches and how it picks a post.

    See also: Web Almanac Data Reveals CMS Plugins Are Setting Technical SEO Standards (Not SEOs).

    The Secrets API would have allowed plugins to save API keys, tokens and more via libsodium encryption, and would have utilized the options tables, which hosts could replace with their own keyring or storage utilizing a secrets.php drop-in.

    Sources indicate that wordPress reverted the API on Nov. 17. The commit points to feedback on the announcement that questioned the design, including whether one API should both write secrets and read the ones a host supplies. Peter Wilson had also found that the API never checked its manage_secrets and manage_network_secrets capabilities when secrets were set. The commit message opens, “Removes the Secrets API from WordPress 7.2 to allow more time for the API to mature before it ships in a future release.”.

    In a recent development, earlier, Ryan McCue, a contributor, had commented that he believes secrets managed outside WordPress should only be readable and never writable to WordPress and that allowing writes to be part of this feature and easy to accomplish makes the API “likely to ossify” around that design. He argued that, under this design, a secrets store backed by hardware security modules offered no additional protection over an already encrypted database. He concluded, “I am a strong -1 on this feature, and I think this should be backed out of core for 7.2 until the above is resolved.”.

    Mullenweg replied, “I agree with @rmccue here.” Two minutes later, he wrote, “It’s also not a great time to be making ourselves a target for very sensitive things like that.”.

    Eric Mann, the writer of the developer note, responded to the encryption point, writing, “Encryption at rest protects against someone walking off with the disk. It does nothing about SQL injection, a leaked mysqldump, a misconfigured backup bucket.” Mann initially wanted to leave the API in 7.2 and referenced a proposed solution for how the AI plugin handles failed write operations, one of the items that was mentioned by McCue.

    After Wilson’s finding, Mann replied, “I’m not excited about it but agree more time will help us ship a more solid foundation here. I’d still like to target at least 7.3 if possible.”.

    The AI plugin version 1.5.0 (released Oct. 29) moved its opt-in Key Encryption experiment into a bundled version of the Secrets API which stores the plugin’s AI service keys. Its maintainers had a pull request open to update it to the version planned for core. After the revert, Jeffrey Paul, who had approved it, wrote that the plugin should “use an approach here that leverages the functionality outside of core” instead. The pull request was still open on Nov. 17, and 1.5.0 was still the latest release.

    See also: When The WordPress Plugin Upgrade Is The Security Risk: Why SEOs Should Pay Attention.

    It has been revealed that wordPress put AI building blocks into core before this release. Roger Montti reported in May that 7.0 shipped four of them, including the WP AI Client and a Connectors screen for AI services. In October, he reported that WordPress had released a canonical MCP Adapter plugin for connecting AI systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

    Industry observers note that wordPress 7.2 is set to add three upcoming read-only abilities, which are registered actions called by other applications. The new read-only abilities allow other applications to query content, users, and WordPress settings. A developer will be able to build an embedding, a numeric representation of text, through the AI client to provide similarity search functionality.

    Sources indicate that in addition to adding the three read-only abilities, the WordPress core team has marked those abilities as exposed to clients such as the WordPress core REST API, MCP, or AI agents. According to the documentation, “Exposure flags do not grant execution permission.” The content query ability requires a logged-in user and checks if the user has read permission for the returned posts. There is right now no MCP server included in the WordPress core.

    According to a post released about version 1.5.0 of the AI plugin, the AI plugin provides versions of these newly introduced abilities that are expected to be identical to the versions “coming in WordPress core with 7.2 this December.” Additionally, the post says there are breaking changes in how existing integrations work because of this update.

    The AI features editors will experience live within the AI plugin itself, where they are currently being tested as opt-in experiments with different requirements; two examples include text-to-speech and revision summaries where content is sent to the site’s selected AI provider. In addition, Content Verification identifies C2PA Content Credentials, a standard for providing provenance information for digital media. However, according to the release post, Content Verification “does not yet perform cryptographic verification” of C2PA Content Credentials. Another feature, MCP Access, decides what the plugin makes available over MCP.

    The AI plugin’s screenshot demonstrates the “Unverified” notice displayed when Content Credentials are detected.

    The AI plugin flags detected Content Credentials as unverified. Screenshot: WordPress AI.

    Supporting broader types of agents in the future is part of plans for the next release. WordPress’s agentic-web proposal says, “Agents can already accomplish a lot with WordPress through WP-CLI, the REST API, and file management. However, these approaches often require local access or more advanced configurations.” The agentic-web proposal plans to implement support for WordPress 7.3 and is planning to develop foundational elements during the 7.2 cycle.

    Admin and login screens in 7.2 separate the combined JavaScript and style sheets they once had into individual assets. According to the roundup, this means each asset is loaded separately by WordPress, which has also included prefetching of the assets needed for the next screen it thinks you’ll be viewing. load-scripts.php and load-styles.php have been deprecated in this version. This change applies to the admin and login screens only.

    The new SVG icons in the admin bar and menu replace the ones previously made available via the Dashicons font. So if your plugins used CSS to add additional styling to those icons’ ::before content, you may want to review them. Beta 5 introduced notification emails when an application password was created. Also according to WordPress, 7.2 aims to include full support for PHP 8.6.

    The preview below shows the upcoming icons in the WordPress admin menu.

    Industry observers note that new icons in the WordPress 7.2 admin menu. Screenshot: WordPress Developer Blog.

    Sources indicate that whether to keep /random/ active is probably the decision most WordPress sites will have to make by Dec. 8. Unless /random/ is turned off, all published posts without a password (including content from a custom post type that is publicly queryable with an archive) can randomly appear. Some commenters on Jorbin’s post thought that would be true for some testimonial or client page custom post types they had created, even though those are not included in the site’s navigation links. First, check which of your custom post types are publicly queryable and have an archive. Then, for any of those custom post types that shouldn’t appear, set 'randomable' => false so that they won’t show up through this method.

    Recent findings suggest that the noindex header isn’t applied to the posts /random/ points to, and the selection made by WordPress doesn’t automatically skip posts an SEO plugin has set to noindex. There was still no response as of Nov. 16 to a commenter who questioned that in the developer notes. People of SEO plugins that prevent access to posts via search engines may want to determine if /random/ will still be able to reach those posts.

    According to recent reports, on sites behind a page cache or CDN, /random/ can return a 404 right after the upgrade. According to the hosting team, that lasts until rewrite rules are flushed, which core does on the first wp-admin request after the upgrade, per site on multisite. On the platform the team tested, a cached 404 stayed after the upgrade until the cache was purged. One tester using shared hosting without a page cache found the rules already in place. To help prevent a stale 404 from being served, purge the page cache after the first admin visit.

    In a recent development, mcCue raised the load that the selection’s random ordering could put on large sites, especially if bots hit /random/ repeatedly. Jorbin stated on Nov. 10 that he had opened a ticket to look at performance on very large sites, and a fix landed on Nov. 17. It looks up random post IDs instead of sorting the archive at random, a method the commit claims “keeps the cost of a request independent of the number of posts”. Archives whose posts are too sparse among the post IDs fall back to a cached pool of up to 1,000 randomly ordered posts. Building that pool still reads every eligible post. Sites with a persistent object cache can reuse the pool for 10 minutes. Mullenweg’s view is that searches and REST calls already offer more ways to strain a site. Teams with large archives can watch for repeated hits on /random/ in their logs after the patch.

    Agency managers running multiple sites will likely handle /random/ in the same way across their entire fleet using a mu-plugin with the correct spelling of the filter.

    Plugin developers can opt public post types out of /random/ where a random visit makes no sense. They’ll also want to check admin CSS for the icon change and patch any integration that calls the content, user, and settings abilities.

    Mullenweg’s /random/ comment about URL structure could lead to changes to the original /random/ proposal. Many commenters (on the developer note) are opposed to the default.

    Sources indicate that when the Secrets API returns, and with what design, is now open too. Sites using the AI plugin’s Key Encryption will need to see how its next release handles the revert.

    According to recent reports, whether /random/ will honor SEO plugins’ noindex settings is still an open question. The release date itself has two values on WordPress.org. The release schedule notes Dec. 8, while the roadmap still lists Dec. 10.

    RC1 on Nov. 17 will include the Field Guide and the 7.2 branch. This should help identify where /random/ ended up. RC2 is set to be released Nov. 24, and RC3 Dec. 1. A dry run and code freeze for Dec. 7 precede the scheduled release on Dec. 8. Agent connection work, broader than just connecting an MCP, along with authorization work in core, is targeted for WordPress 7.3.

    To test if /random/ can access your content and how this impacts caching, you’ll need to install RC1 onto a staging version of your website.

    The Cornell Daily Sun saw traffic spike by almost 500% in September.

    It has been revealed that RELATED ARTICLESearch traffic has declined so much that some publishers are considering opting out of Google entirelyNeel DhaneshaJuly 22, 2026We’ve now been publishing roundups of local newspaper traffic for a full year, so we can compare this year’s traffic to last year’s. Almost across the board, local newspapers are seeing traffic decline as Google referrals drop. For July, August, and September, traffic to the most-visited sites is lower than at this time last year, according to our Similarweb data.

    According to recent reports, RELATED ARTICLEHow did newspapers in places like Harrisburg, Birmingham, and Syracuse become some of America’s most-read online?Joshua BentonJuly 23, 2025A good example is Advance Local’s Harrisburg Patriot-News, PennLive.com. Josh has written about Advance publications punching above their weight in traffic. They still are: Advance outlets like AL.com, Mlive.com, and NJ.com, among others, continued to feature prominently in the top sites by estimated monthly visits in July, August, and September. In August 2026, PennLive’s traffic growth stood out even among Advance peers; it gained 3.6 million visits in August compared to July, a 78% spike. But in total, PennLive saw a little over 8.2 million monthly visits for August 2026 — down from about 12.5 million in August 2025.

    Recent findings suggest that still, publishers large and small are finding ways to bring more readers to their sites. In August, the Bozeman Daily Chronicle grew its traffic by about 96,000 monthly visits, a 49% jump. Managing editor Jack Reaney attributed the growth to the newspaper launching a new website Aug. 3 designed for improved functionality, with “fewer, more intentional news categories,” lighter page design for faster load times, and a more modern layout. The Chronicle is one of more than 150 newspapers owned by Adams MultiMedia. The parent company is rolling out the new website design across its newspapers, but Bozeman was the “guinea pig,” Reaney said.

    In Florida, Cape Coral Breeze, a small weekly, saw its traffic spike about 139% in August. The network of local weeklies has tried to adopt a daily, real-time mindset after decades of posting once a week, Breeze Newspapers publisher Ray Eckenrode told me. The August spike was driven by participation in Cape Coral Breeze’s “Best of Cape Coral” contest, where readers vote on favorite local businesses in more than 200 categories. According to the team’s internal count, a little over 150,000 “Best of” votes were cast this year, up from 92,000 last year. The team made an effort this year to “drive traffic to our homepage first to reach the contest voting page to expose some of those casual website owners to our news coverage,” Eckenrode stated, and had some success with that strategy.

    In September, The Cornell Daily Sun gained 1 million visits, almost a 500% jump from August, when it broke the story of the Cornell 7 lawsuit (and published an editorial naming the defendants). Other local news sites in New York also saw meaningful growth in September; traffic to NNY360.com jumped 84%, while the Gannett-owned Democrat and Chronicle gained about 762,000 visits, a 35% jump.

    Industry observers note that on the opposite coast, the San-Jose-based Mercury News gained around 690,000 monthly visits in September, a 14% jump. “Our traffic is volatile like everyone else’s, but we had a strong September mainly because a couple of stories performed very well,” said Annika Toernqvist, MediaNews Group’s managing editor for digital for Northern California. Environmental beat reporter Paul Rogers‘ story about a fresh California law that will ban watering artificial turf “performed exceptionally well on Google and Google Discovery”; 62% of traffic to the story came from search. Stories about the local impact of new state laws consistently do well with the outlet’s readers, according to Toernqvist, and this was “a hot topic with a strong headline.” The story was also the top subscription converter in September. Another story by Rogers covering the proposed renaming of Fremont State Park also drove traffic that month; 86% came from search, mostly from Google Discovery.

    Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, celebrity reporter Martha Ross‘ story about a new book on King Charles’ valet performed well in part thanks to a bump from…the Drudge Report. (“Yes, the Drudge Report still drives traffic,” Toernqvist stated; it accounted for 43% of visits to that story.).

    Over the next two years, NPR will address a longstanding listener plea: improving its app.

    During a November 12 board of directors meeting, NPR CEO Katherine Maher said the organization will rebuild its digital offerings to be a “service-first, app-first destination” as part of NPR’s 2027-2029 strategic strategy, Current reported on Thursday. One goal of the plan is to reach “five million weekly active owners on its platforms by 2029” and “to build a monthly engaged digital audience of 40 million.” According to Current, Maher said that the NPR network — which includes more than 200 member radio stations — presently reaches 39 million weekly listeners across broadcast and digital, but the “total potential addressable audience, weekly consumers of news, information and culture who are open to our work, is roughly 153 million Americans. That is nearly four times our current reach.”.

    Sources indicate that in Apple’s App Store, NPR’s app has a 4.7-star rating and more than 78,000 reviews, of which the majority are positive. But reviewers have quibbles.

    According to recent reports, bryan Moffett, NPR’s senior vice president of transformation, said NPR+, the broadcaster’s subscription program, brought in $8 million in the 2026 fiscal year, up from $5.5 million in 2025. (NPR+ is available with a donation of $8 a month or more, and offers perks like podcasts without ads.) Maher said new investment in the app will help reach younger audiences and shift NPR’s “median audience age from 60-plus toward 40-plus.”.

    “We love radio, but we have been so wildly successful there that we’ve largely exhausted its further financial growth,” Maher told the board. “And as it shrinks, we must invert our revenue engine to ensure sustainability across all of our platforms, including radio, but to build a wider funnel through digital offerings, third-party platforms, and new investments in marketing and communication that will tell our story and share our value with the world.”.

    According to recent reports, RELATED ARTICLENPR, the quintessential audio news brand, adapts to a video-first futureSarah ScireSeptember 29, 2026Overhauling the app is just one part of NPR’s strategy to keep up with customers’ changing consumption preferences. In September, Sarah Scire reported on the broadcaster leaning into video podcasts with the acquisition of Kevin Roose and Casey Newton’s technology podcast Machine Gods. NPR chief operating officer Ryan Merkley told Current in June that NPR was already working on redesigning the app to better serve member stations and their listeners.

    According to recent reports, “Fix the app,” departing public editor Kelly McBride told NPR leaders during the meeting. “It’s not a great experience for the audience and it’s key to moving forward, but you guys seem like you’re on it. So I won’t dwell on that.”.

    According to recent reports, nieman Lab requested a copy of the approved strategic blueprint but did not receive it by publication time. Read the full story in Current here.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    Sources indicate that we're looking for a Developer Relations Engineer to join our team and help more developers discover, learn, and build with Supabase. You'll create high-impact content, build real-world projects, and represent Supabase across communities and events. If you're equally energized by writing code and teaching others, this is the role for you.

    Sources indicate that supabase is growing fast with 350,000+ developers, 1,000+ OSS contributors, and a thriving open source ecosystem. Our people are builders, startup founders, weekend hackers, and engineers scaling to millions of users. DevRel is how we meet them where they are: through content, community, and code.

    According to recent reports, we're building a community of communities that brings together developers from many backgrounds, including first-time open source contributors. As a DevRel Engineer, you'll be a bridge between Supabase and the broader developer ecosystem, helping people get started, go deep, and feel connected.

    Make content — Publish compelling technical content, especially video, to help developers learn Supabase swiftly.

    According to recent reports, build demos and tutorials — Ship real-world apps using Supabase and tools like Next.js, React, and Stripe. Write guides that others can follow and remix.

    According to recent reports, represent Supabase — Speak at meetups, livestream builds, and engage with the developer ecosystem. You'll be a visible and trusted voice of the platform.

    Support and grow the community — Celebrate contributors, answer questions, highlight cool projects, and bring developer feedback to the team.

    Collaborate across the firm — Work with engineering, product, and growth to amplify launches, prioritize content, and reduce friction for newly introduced owners.

    You've built full-stack apps and enjoy sharing your knowledge.

    You create content that makes people want to open their code editor.

    You're equally comfortable writing a video script and TypeScript.

    You're energized by community whether it's on Discord, Twitter, YouTube, or in person.

    You're self-directed, organized, and excited to contribute to open source.

    Strong engineering skills, especially with JavaScript or TypeScript, Postgres, and modern frontend frameworks (React, Svelte, Vue, etc.).

    Experience creating technical content (written or video).

    Comfortable representing a product publicly (on camera, on stage, or online).

    A growing audience on YouTube, Twitch, or Twitter.

    Prior experience in DevRel or open source.

    Recent findings suggest that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the organization. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Sources indicate that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

    Industry observers note that once a year, the entire tech giant gathers in a latest city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    In a recent development, supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    Latest Update: WordPress 7.1.5 Security Release Fixes 18 Vulnerabilities via @sejournal, @martinibuster

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (373 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • WordPress announced the release of version 7.1.5, a security revision that fixes 18 vulnerabilities plus two security improvements.
    • WordPress 7.1.5 fixes 20 concerns covering a range of vulnerabilities across WordPress core.
    • Recent findings suggest that the first one that stands out is an unauthenticated privilege escalation vulnerability affecting the Template Part block attributes which could lead to remote code execution (RCE), a type of flaw that can result in a site takeover.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    WordPress announced the release of version 7.1.5, a security revision that fixes 18 vulnerabilities plus two security improvements. The update addresses several types of vulnerabilities, including cross-site scripting and SQL injection, as well as an unauthenticated flaw that could lead to remote code execution.

    WordPress 7.1.5 fixes 20 concerns covering a range of vulnerabilities across WordPress core. One of the vulnerabilities in particular stands out because it could lead to remote code execution (RCE), a type of flaw that can result in a site takeover.

    Recent findings suggest that the first one that stands out is an unauthenticated privilege escalation vulnerability affecting the Template Part block attributes which could lead to remote code execution (RCE), a type of flaw that can result in a site takeover. There is no authentication required to exploit this vulnerability, and it could lead to RCE. That combination is the worst-case scenario for a CMS.

    A remote code execution (RCE) is a vulnerability that enables an attacker to run their own code on someone else’s server from somewhere else, usually over the internet. For a WordPress site, that means the attacker can make the web server execute commands of their choosing. From there they can read or change files and make entries to the database, create admin accounts, install backdoors, or inject malware.

    Recent findings suggest that multisite Administrator to Super Admin takeover (Customizer menu previews). This vulnerability requires an Administrator account, but on a multisite installation that means that an attacker who achieves admin level credential on one site can attain control of the entire network of sites.

    Industry observers note that unauthenticated stored XSS via shortcode attributes in comments. No login is needed to exploit it. Stored XSS is a type of flaw that can run malicious code in the browser of anyone who views the affected comment, including administrators, which can lead to account takeover.

    Two SQL injection vulnerabilities:.

    WordPress urges site owners to update to version 7.1.5 immediately to address security vulnerabilities. The update is available through the WordPress dashboard or as a download, with automatic updates supported. Security fixes are also available for older affected WordPress versions, although only the latest version is actively supported.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    It has been revealed that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    It has been revealed that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    At Cambridge Day, “having full-time reporters was transformative.” Our latest traffic rankings for nonprofit news outlets.

    Is something in the water in Nieman Lab’s home state? In our latest quarterly ranking of nonprofit news outlets, eight Massachusetts nonprofit news outlets enjoyed significant jumps in traffic. Massachusetts is the state that appeared most frequently in this quarter’s data, followed by California (7), Michigan (4), and New York (4).

    Four of those Massachusetts outlets largely attributed the traffic spikes to hyperlocal stories that served specific reader needs and curiosities.

    According to recent reports, cambridge Day garnered 160,000 visits in July, a 60% increase from June. Editor Michael Fitzgerald (a 2011 Nieman Fellow) mentioned the publication’s top story that month was about the city halting a multifamily home demolition. Other major stories covered the sale of two independent movie theaters and a July 4 shooting.

    Reader support allowed Cambridge Day to hire a full-time reporter in June, along with four summer intern reporters whose positions were funded through their universities. In July, Fitzgerald noted, the news outlet published 32 stories per week.

    According to recent reports, “Having full-time reporters was transformative. News does not pay a living wage to freelancers,” Fitzgerald remarked in an email. “They have to pay their bills by doing other things, so they just aren’t as available as full-time reporters. We made the decision to hire a second reporter, who started in late August. We took a bit of a risk and brought on [a] freelancer as a six-month editorial fellow. I cut my freelance budget in half and have rejiggered some other expenses to make this less risky.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Lexington Observer got 62,000 visits in August, a 47% increase from the previous month. Executive director Lauren Feeney said the August story with the most traffic was about how a resident-led complaint delayed the construction of what would be the most expensive high school in the country.

    In a recent development, election coverage ahead of the midterms also resonated. “Our coverage of two little-known progressive candidates running to unseat [Rep. Katherine Clark] from the left got a ton of traffic, I believe because hardly anything else had been written about them, so readers came to our site not just from Lexington but from the entire 5th Congressional district, including Cambridge,” Feeney stated. “My takeaway from this is to keep focusing on undercovered and hyperlocal stories, and not spend a lot of resources on stories that are already widely covered.”.

    It has been revealed that august was also a newsy month for the Marblehead Current. With 156 published stories in August, the Current’s traffic increased by 53% compared to July. Cofounder and reporter Leigh Blander said her investigation into the city’s road conditions sparked engagement on Facebook and Instagram, driving pageviews. Other stories that resonated with readers covered a boat crash, a seal carcass, racist graffiti, and education coverage during back-to-school season.

    CommonWealth Beacon, which covers statewide politics and policy, saw its September traffic increase by 37% over August. Editor Laura Colarusso attributed the growth to the publication’s coverage of Massachusetts’ nine ballot questions.

    Industry observers note that “Our ballot question guide brought a lot of new readers to our site and strengthened our relationship with many of the hyperlocal news organizations that regularly republish our stories,” Colarusso stated. “We’ve not made any concrete changes yet, but that experience has led to discussions around what tools we can leverage to create a deeper relationship with people who are coming to our site for the first time.”.

    Other Massachusetts-based outlets in this quarter’s data included The Latest Bedford Light, The Newton Beacon, the Plymouth Independent, and The Belmont Voice.

    Other outlets with notable gains this quarter:.

    Votebeat, the national nonprofit covering U.S. elections, saw a 154% increase in website visits in July, up from 62,600 visits in June. Growth and community editor Lauren Aguirre said that jump was the result of publishing a scoop that President Trump had fired all of the members of the Election Assistance Commission.

    That story alone brought in 110,047 pageviews, and 17% of those came from Reddit.

    Recent findings suggest that “With the demise of Twitter, we’ve really been leaning into Reddit and other spaces where political nerds like to hang out,” Aguirre said. “The outsized attention this story received on Reddit is absolutely due to our continued presence over there. Before Votebeat began posting on Reddit a few years ago, we’d almost never be linked in communities like this.”.

    Shelterforce, a nonprofit publication covering affordable housing, saw its July traffic increase by 85%, from 43,100 in June to 79,800. Director of editorial operations Lillian Ortiz attributed the spike to a story about a federal government proposal that put rental assistance at risk. That story received 18,000 pageviews and is one of the site’s top stories of the year. Ortiz also suspects that more readers are becoming listeners as Shelterforce grows its offering of audio versions of its stories. So far this year, Shelterforce has logged 30,000 listens, a 16% increase over 2025.

    Sources indicate that “Many of our authors read their stories, and that has helped us reach newly introduced audiences and give people another way to engage with our work,” Ortiz remarked. “While the audio is embedded with stories on our website, people can also listen to us on other audio-streaming platforms. We also offer AI-generated audio for stories that aren’t read by a person.”.

    The Buckeye Flame, which covers LGBTQ+ complications in Ohio, got 45,000 unique visits in July, up from 25,000 in June. Editor Ken Schneck noted that the Flame continued to report on its usual beats, including state politics and rural issues, and no particular story drove a surge in traffic.

    “The July traffic is so affirming because we literally changed nothing about how we do what we do,” Schneck mentioned. “Our goal is to publish a upcoming piece every weekday and to amplify topics ranging from policy and legislation to rural coverage to queer joy, and that’s exactly what happened for us in July.”.

    It has been revealed that the Imprint, a national nonprofit covering the child welfare and juvenile justice systems, saw an 82% increase in its August traffic over July, from 68,500 to 124,800. Co-executive director Christie Renick remarked one story — about the state of Utah revoking the license of a mental health treatment facility following complaints from advocates including Paris Hilton — drove much of that traffic and resulted in nearly 25,000 pageviews. (Renick couldn’t find any evidence that Hilton herself shared the story.).

    Recent findings suggest that the Juneau Independent saw a 40% increase in visits from July to August, and a 31% increase from August to September. In real numbers, the Independent went from 41,800 visits in July to 77,300 by the end of September.

    Industry observers note that the news of the spike was a surprise to editor Mark Sabbatini, who makes up one-fourth of the newsroom that rolled out in June 2025 to cover Alaska’s capital. Sabbatini attributed the August traffic growth to the Independent’s coverage of a glacial lake outburst flood, “a disaster-level event Juneau has experienced every August for the past four years.”.

    According to recent reports, “We see it as a core responsibility to provide the best possible coverage before, during and after those floods, and our staff worked around the clock to provide updates as flooding peaked and during its aftermath. In addition to high local readership, that coverage is also read, cited, and republished elsewhere,” Sabbatini stated. “It seems fair to state the Independent and [public radio station] KTOO are now considered Juneau’s primary news sources and what people were relying on for critical information as an emergency situation unfolded.”.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Realworkfromanywhere ↗ Open Full Page

    Attorney, New Verticals at Atticus

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, at any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government.
    • According to recent reports, atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured person in crisis to get the life-changing aid they deserve.
    • It has been revealed that so far, we've helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10B in life-changing aid — and earned over 20,000+ five-star reviews.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, at any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government. The right assistance could transform their lives. But today, most never get it.

    According to recent reports, atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured person in crisis to get the life-changing aid they deserve. In the last six years, we've become the leading platform connecting people with disabilities to government benefits. We’re also quickly scaling an injury practice to help victims of accidents, misconduct, and violence get compensation from insurance.

    It has been revealed that so far, we've helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10B in life-changing aid — and earned over 20,000+ five-star reviews. And we're just getting started.

    We've raised more than $100 million from top VC firms like Forerunner, GV (Google Ventures), and True Ventures, with ambitions to create a category defining business assisting Americans in need.

    Each month, tens of thousands of Americans seek our help for a single legal matter – applying for Social Security Disability, filing a Workers’ Compensation claim – but many of these clients are actually eligible for additional aid without ever knowing it.

    It has been revealed that your job as Lead Attorney, Fresh Verticals is to help us do right by these clients, helping them claim additional benefits through the social safety net. You’ll oversee the team of intake specialists who speak with clients who have secondary claims, evaluating the case facts and whether to connect them with an Atticus attorney or local attorney to provide legal advice and potentially take on their case.

    Industry observers note that this is a job that straddles the line between practicing the law and growing a business. It requires developing a strong understanding of multiple fields of law, and being able to accurately identify when we can help and when we cannot. But even more importantly, this job requires you to be an incredibly strong operator: you need to keep the major picture in mind and stay laser-focused on how we can achieve our goals, oftentimes finding outside-the-box ways to accomplish them. You will report to our General Manager of Fresh Verticals and work closely with our CEO and Managing Attorney.

    On any given day, you’ll spend your time:.

    Speaking with severely injured clients trying to rebuild their lives after a catastrophic accident.

    Sourcing and vetting local counsel in individual markets, holding a high bar for representation quality and ending relationships that fall below it.

    Working with our data and insights team to identify existing clients who may have unrecognized claims in adjacent fields of law, and setting the standard for which ancillary cases we take on.

    Building the playbook for claim types we haven't handled before, starting by screening cases yourself and eventually creating the protocol our intake specialists will run at scale.

    This is a rare opportunity for an attorney to join a profitable and growing public-interest law firm and take on one of our biggest priorities as a firm.

    You can understand the nuances of various contingency fields of law and can apply them to a variety of cases (including Social Security Disability, Workers’ Compensation, Personal Injury, and more) – you don’t need to be an expert today, but you should be a fast learner.

    You can empathize with anyone and quickly build rapport and relationships while exercising good judgment, both with our clients and local counsel at law firms across the country.

    You have strong instincts and judgment as an operator – you can run effective and efficient processes, and you don’t let them run you.

    You have a demonstrated commitment to doing good and helping people.

    You’ve built a track record as a great people manager – you know how to motivate talent and hold a high bar for output.

    You have meaningful work experience outside of serving as a lawyer, ideally at a startup or other fast-paced, agile environment (e.g., a business operations team).

    According to recent reports, we are strongly committed to building a diverse team. If you're from a background that's underrepresented in tech, we'd love to meet you.

    This role offers a unique chance to join a startup that has strong traction (substantial funding, well-respected backers, tremendous growth, and many happy customers) but is still small enough that you can have a huge impact and play a role in shaping our success.

    We're a certified B Corporation tackling a critical social problem. Our mission to help people in need drives everything we do, and your work here will touch many lives.

    We offer competitive pay — including equity — and generous benefits:.

    Medical and dental insurance with 100% of employees and their families premiums covered.

    15 vacation days & ~20 paid holidays each year (including two weeks at end-of-year).

    $1,000 reimbursable stipend for education and training outside of work.

    Up to $1,200/year student loan repayment assistance.

    401(k) match and optional HSA/FSA.

    Humble, thoughtful, smart, fun colleagues.

    It has been revealed that we anticipate the base salary band for this role will be between $140,000 and $175,000 in addition to equity and benefits. The salary at offer will be determined by a number of factors such as candidate's experience, knowledge, skills and abilities, as well as internal equity among our team.

    This job is fully remote and we’re committed to empowering everyone with flexibility. Work remotely, and travel to LA (on the manufacturer dime) as needed to be with your colleagues – usually quarterly, plus offsites. We care a lot about building a great culture and we think some interactions need to happen in person, so we put a lot of thought into retreats, offsites, and other ways to gather.

    RELATED ARTICLEThe Latest York Times will launch a local newsletter pilot in the Twin Cities next monthSophie CulpepperJuly 9, 2026This year’s State of Local News Report from Medill was grim. But in the Twin Cities, Neal St. Anthony writes, a rich local news ecosystem offers a more hopeful picture. The metro area of more than 3 million people is home to The Minnesota Star Tribune, public radio powerhouse MPR, local TV stations, and multiple successful nonprofit startups, from nearly two-decade-old MinnPost to Sahan Journal (whose founder, Mukhtar Ibrahim, also launched The Somali Brief this fall). Axios has published an Axios Local newsletter for the Twin Cities since 2021, and this summer, The New York Times launched its own Twin Cities local newsletter.

    RELATED ARTICLEWith Washington Post Local diminished, other news sites step up their D.C. coverageSophie CulpepperMarch 5, 2026The question this ecosystem raises, according to St. Anthony, is “whether the Twin Cities represents the potential future of local news in metros across the country: a robust ecosystem with no dominant mass-market player but more news outlets tailored to smaller, niche audiences with narrower but deep interests.” (That description brings to mind other urban media markets where a diffuse ecosystem of smaller, newer players have stepped up as legacy media pulls back.).

    “There is a healthy degree of vitality in local news in the Twin Cities. The story elsewhere is ‘news deserts’ and little original journalism,” University of Minnesota professor Benjamin Toff told St. Anthony. While local institutions like the Star Tribune have survived, he added, “it’s not immune to industry forces, including the veritable disappearance of print.”.

    In a recent development, A few highlights from St. Anthony’s piece for Medill:.

    On MPR: After the 2025 rescission of federal funding for public media, Minnesota Public Radio lost about $6 million. But MPR, like other public broadcasters, was able to turn the rescission into a highly successful fundraising campaign. Its 2026 fiscal revenue rose 5% to $119 million, and it grew to 172,000 paying members, a record.

    #8171. After gutting newsrooms, McClatchy plans to rebuild itself around AI

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2156 w)

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    After gutting newsrooms, McClatchy plans to rebuild itself around AI

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2156 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • The local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old manufacturer is no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    The local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old manufacturer is no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month.

    Two months after McClatchy Media laid off more than 90 journalists nationwide, executives at the storied local newspaper chain offered a blunt assessment of its future.

    The award-winning local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old organization was no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month, and its survival depended on a wholesale reinvention — centered entirely around artificial intelligence.

    According to recent reports, from the rollout of fresh lifestyle websites that feature AI-generated articles and sponsored content to legal review and finance, executives revealed how AI is now integrated into virtually every part of the manufacturer. The demonstration comes after McClatchy, one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates, carried out deep staff cuts in September at the Miami Herald, The Kansas City Star, and more than a dozen other local news outlets. An anonymous “person close to the executive decision-making” told The New York Times the layoffs were not about AI and were instead about “business performance in some areas.”.

    A companywide blueprint presented during the meeting highlights how McClatchy is systematically outsourcing the infrastructure for local news to AI agents — and rebranding around lifestyle verticals for sports fans, outdoor enthusiasts, and true-crime junkies.

    Dubbed “Project Catalyst,” the companywide restructure will create an “AI-native operating model” that takes “repeated tasks off of humans” and embeds AI agents “directly into the daily workflow,” Jeff Dorsey, McClatchy’s chief operating officer, said at the town hall. Dorsey described the initiative as an effort to automate “non-core as well as core functions,” “get rid of things that just don’t offer the same value” they once did, and “provide cash, frankly, to keep the business afloat.”.

    McClatchy, which operates 29 daily newspapers across 14 states, didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment.

    Central to the rebrand is the launch of four upcoming websites: Crime Hunter, a site devoted to “real-life crime and justice”; Saltwater South, which “celebrates the places, people and experiences that make the coastal South unlike anywhere else”; Camp & Country, a “national outdoor destination”; and Student Section, billed as “the home of the college sports fan.”.

    Each of the sites is “powered by Trend Hunter,” a organization McClatchy acquired in 2024 that uses AI “to glean insights into consumer trends” and sell consumer goods like $33.91 rosemary oil “to support a healthy scalp environment,” a $249 red light therapy cap to regrow hair “without the hassle of messy serums” and $34.99 “MAGIC Mushroom Coffee” for “clarity, balance and natural energy.”.

    Recent findings suggest that little discussed, however, were the organization’s local news ambitions. Kristine Sherred, chair of the Washington State NewsGuild and the food and dining reporter at The News Tribune in Tacoma, Washington, remarked that she and other journalists were left to wonder “why we were even invited.”.

    “Our takeaway was that it wasn’t about news,” Sherred said. “The future McClatchy appears to be building does not seem aligned with the mission of journalism.”.

    The meeting this month offered the clearest roadmap to date about McClatchy’s all-in approach to AI as one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates navigates traffic declines, shifting consumer habits, and heavy debt obligations. It also comes at a critical moment for a media industry that seeks to modernize with AI — technology simultaneously blamed for gutting web traffic and touted as a tool to cut costs.

    It has been revealed that “There is no sector that has not been disrupted this year by AI — everyone is going through extraordinary disruption,” Hunter noted. Through a laser focus on AI-powered efficiencies, he said, the tech giant can turn around its fortunes. “We can win — not with yesterday’s solutions, though.”.

    For McClatchy, which has undergone aggressive cost-cutting efforts since it was acquired by New Jersey-based hedge fund Chatham Asset Management in 2020, its pivot toward AI-generated content over the last year has been met with internal pushback and, from some readers, ridicule.

    In May, journalists at The Sacramento Bee, the Miami Herald, and other McClatchy-owned papers withheld their names from articles that were produced with its “content scaling agent,” a chatbot that repackages human-written news articles at varying lengths for different audiences — complete with reporters’ names.

    Similar resistance has played out at other news outlets. Earlier this month, for example, reporters at the Akron Beacon Journal in Ohio withheld their bylines for two weeks to protest a tool that generates AI summaries of articles that, the journalists allege, undermines their work and provides readers false information.

    Many news organizations prohibit the publication of AI-generated articles. But for McClatchy, they’ve become a core part of its business strategy and, according to Hunter, a key part of its “organization-wide effort to agentify the entire enterprise.” During a contentious virtual meeting in May, Hunter pleaded with skeptical journalists to get on board or find another job.

    Anyone at McClatchy can now build AI tools to support their workflows, Rajiv Pant, McClatchy’s chief product and engineering officer, mentioned earlier this month.

    “In every one of these, humans are at the command center, they aren’t just checking the technology’s work,” Pant said. “They set the direction, make the calls and own the results. The technology lets each one of them do more of the work that only they can do.”.

    In a recent development, trend Hunter content — including AI-generated posts — now appears regularly across McClatchy’s local publications and social media feeds, including articles with little connection to the communities those outlets have historically served. Recent examples include a post about winter “barn jackets” in the Miami Herald and a feature about collegiate football in Texas for the Kansas City Star.

    Other posts highlight obscure beauty products and questionable health trends, including how nugget ice “has become the craze worth understanding,” how saunas have “reshaped social wellness,” and “what your poop color, shape and frequency say about your gut health.”.

    Or, as one Kansas City Star reporter put it, the layoffs have created news websites where it’s “city reporters out, shitty reporters in.”.

    “They’re trying to kind of go toward these buzzy-type topics instead of local journalism that holds people to account,” stated the reporter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to retaliation concerns.

    Industry observers note that readers, an overwhelming majority of whom are skeptical of AI use in newsrooms, have also taken notice. In a post on X, one social media user wrote that “people want the news” not “AI generated slop.” Another called into question McClatchy’s decision to publish an article — across numerous local news brands — about why the actress Scarlett Johansson “changed her magnesium supplement routine after a spray left her feet feeling dry.”.

    Recent findings suggest that this AI slop is what McClatchy forced a bunch of its newspapers to publish in unison a few weeks ago. Who needs real human reporters when you can have this? https://t.co/Z82Vg67WtH.

    — James (@jameslineky) September 10, 2026.

    Given the rapid spread of AI-generated content online, McClatchy executives see the brand credibility of its legacy publications as a differentiator. Over time, Hunter said, the market will reward trust — and McClatchy is well positioned to capitalize on its local news audiences.

    “It is important that we have credible, accurate and relevant content,” Hunter said. “We are not running from our standards, but we’re running toward a latest model to help customers make better decisions.”.

    Industry observers note that in recent months, as much as 20% of articles published by McClatchy newspapers were AI-generated, according to data from AI-detection tech giant Originality.ai. (AI detection tools like Originality are imprecise in distinguishing synthetic writing from human-authored content.) Rather than building fresh audiences, McClatchy’s use of AI-generated content could erode trust among readers, said Jon Gillham, Originality’s founder and CEO.

    Such a reality is already playing out in Washington, noted Sherred of the Washington State NewsGuild. Sherred’s union went on strike in May to demand “ethical limits” around the organization’s use of AI. The guild said in a statement at the time it was negotiating for “freedom to write hard-hitting news stories that take time, and not be punished if we don’t churn out clickbait.”.

    It has been revealed that “We hear this from people in the community all the time: They don’t want short snippets, they don’t want rehashed work and they don’t want AI telling them the news,” Sherred stated. “The only way you get high-quality local news is by having high-quality local reporters actually out there making it.”.

    Less than a week after McClatchy laid off journalists nationwide in September, executives sent the remaining staff an emoji-laced email announcing “fresh talent”: several executives, two reporters and three editors for its “Content Innovation Lab” — the engine behind its latest AI-powered lifestyle verticals.

    A recent job listing for innovation lab writers notes the “company’s future depends” on an embrace of AI and the innovation lab is its “next-generation approach to content” where emerging technologies are leveraged to “fuel experimentation and productivity.”.

    According to recent reports, “From barbecue to bourbon, water sports to hiking, and golf to college sports, we are going to develop a steady stream of reader-focused, high-quality content for national and regional audiences,” according to the job listing. Producers will use AI to launch fresh brands “tied to dedicated communities of interest around travel, food, outdoor recreation, sports and even crime.”.

    The insights into the firm’s future editorial direction come on the heels of its steepest staff reduction in years, with layoffs of investigative reporters, government watchdogs, and other journalists focused on local news.

    Recent findings suggest that “The city of Tacoma no longer has a city reporter,” Sherred said. “What’s the purpose of a local paper if you have no one covering your local government?”.

    It has been revealed that hired to lead the Content Innovation Lab is Patrick Stiegman, a 20-year ESPN digital veteran who, during the meeting this month, turned to sports media lingo to describe the goal behind Saltwater South, Camp & Country, and its other AI-powered lifestyle brands. By “cultivating passionate fans” around obsessive lifestyle niches, he said, the company seeks to leverage reader data “and monetization opportunities” to guide coverage decisions.

    Perhaps nobody put McClatchy’s pivot in starker terms than Ariel Storch, recently hired to lead an AI-powered rebrand of its video strategy.

    “We make entertainment — not content, entertainment,” Storch said during the Nov. 6 meeting. “Think about a late-night show. Nobody tunes in to be informed, they tune in to laugh. The by-product is you leave knowing about a new movie, a new book, a new product.”.

    According to recent reports, building newly introduced audiences is critical as the tech giant works to claw itself out of debt, stated Joe Settineri, McClatchy’s chief financial officer. Stabilizing McClatchy’s core business is necessary, he said, for the Content Innovation Lab and its other AI initiatives to be successful.

    “Today, most of that profitability is already spoken for because, like most companies, we have a sizable amount of debt,” Settineri remarked. “Like a loan on a house, we have to pay it down or you lose the house.”.

    Mark Keierleber is an independent investigative journalist who most recently reported on media, bias, and algorithms for Straight Arrow News.
