    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    It has been revealed that we're looking for a detail-oriented, driven Senior Accountant to join our Accounting team at an exciting time of growth for Supabase. As we continue to scale, we're expanding the team to add experience, spread responsibilities, and strengthen the processes that keep our financials accurate and timely. This is a hands-on role with real ownership and a lot of autonomy.

    It has been revealed that in this role, you'll support the month-end close, perform analytics on financial results, assist with external audit and tax requests, and take on ad-hoc projects. You'll collaborate across Finance and the wider company, including FP&A, People/Payroll, and Legal, and work with our external audit, tax, and technical accounting partners, while contributing to the continuous improvement of our processes and controls. This role is open to candidates based in North America.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

    Own key areas of the monthly, quarterly, and annual close within your assigned areas, preparing workpapers, journal entries, account reconciliations, flux analysis, and accruals in accordance with US GAAP.

    Perform detailed analytics over financial results to confirm completeness and accuracy, and investigate and communicate discrepancies promptly.

    Partner with FP&A, People/Payroll, Legal, and other teams to understand business processes, ensure proper accounting, and resolve reconciling differences.

    Support external audits and tax requests, serving as a point of contact and coordinating with external partners.

    Prepare ad-hoc analyses and support reporting requirements.

    Take initiative to recommend and implement process improvements that simplify, standardize, and streamline how we work.

    Participate in special projects, including process and system improvements.

    Handle day-to-day operational accounting activities with a high level of accuracy.

    Have 5+ years of progressive accounting experience, ideally a mix of public accounting (Significant 4 preferred) and private industry.

    Have a CPA or equivalent (preferred).

    Have a strong technical accounting background and solid knowledge of US GAAP.

    Have ERP experience, and experience in tech or high-growth organization accounting is a plus.

    Are willing to roll up your sleeves and dig into the details.

    Communicate clearly, both in writing and verbally, and are comfortable building relationships at all levels of the organization, including senior leadership and audit partners.

    Are self-motivated and proactive in identifying problems and proposing solutions.

    Are organized and able to manage multiple priorities and deadlines, and can switch gears promptly in a fast-paced, high-growth environment.

    Work well both independently and collaboratively, are comfortable in async teams, and navigate ambiguity with ease.

    Are energized by improving processes.

    In a recent development, we know not everyone will meet every qualification on day one. If you're excited about this role and want to grow with us, we encourage you to apply.

    Industry observers note that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the manufacturer. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

    Industry observers note that once a year, the entire company gathers in a latest city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 17, Chrome 158 rolls out to the majority of desktop and mobile users and drops support for client-side XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations).
    • For years, WordPress core and major SEO plugins, including Yoast SEO, Rank Math, and All in One SEO (AIOSEO), have referenced an .xsl stylesheet inside their XML sitemaps.
    • Without XSLT support, opening a WordPress sitemap in Chrome 158 displays raw, unstyled XML markup alongside a browser console and page warning.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Nov. 17, Chrome 158 rolls out to the majority of desktop and mobile users and drops support for client-side XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations).

    For years, WordPress core and major SEO plugins, including Yoast SEO, Rank Math, and All in One SEO (AIOSEO), have referenced an .xsl stylesheet inside their XML sitemaps. When a person opened a sitemap URL in a browser, Chrome executed that XSLT file to transform the underlying XML code into a clean, clickable HTML table.

    Without XSLT support, opening a WordPress sitemap in Chrome 158 displays raw, unstyled XML markup alongside a browser console and page warning.

    Screenshot from author, November 2026.

    Search engines do not use XSLT. Googlebot, Bingbot, and other web crawlers fetch and parse the raw XML nodes (, ) at the source. Crawlers avoid browser-side stylesheets, meaning indexing, crawl efficiency, and search rankings remain unaffected.

    Sources indicate that because Chrome 158 lands while Google’s November core patch, which began on Nov. 10, is still rolling, site owners and clients checking their domains during routine ranking audits may panic when they see raw XML in place of the familiar formatted table.

    Depending on your site configuration, WordPress serves its sitemap index from one of two primary URLs:.

    If you open either URL in Chrome 158 or a newer release, seeing a wall of XML tags confirms the browser skipped the XSLT stylesheet, not that the sitemap file is corrupt or broken.

    Screenshot from author, November 2026.

    To verify, or prove to a nervous client, that Google reads the sitemap without trouble, check Google Search Console:.

    As long as Search Console reports “Success,” Google parses the XML structure without error.

    It has been revealed that XML sitemaps exist for machine consumption, and search engine bots read the underlying and tags. Dropping visual styling changes nothing about URL discovery, crawl budget, or search visibility.

    Because Chrome 158 arrives alongside the November core update, clients or stakeholders who inspect their sitemap URLs will spot unformatted XML code and assume a site outage or plugin failure caused ranking fluctuations.

    Chrome logs a deprecation warning in DevTools whenever a page invokes an .xsl stylesheet. Automated site-health crawlers or QA tools that monitor browser console errors may flag sitemap URLs until plugins or WordPress core drop the stylesheet reference.

    Editors and junior marketers who relied on opening /sitemap_index.xml in Chrome as a quick directory of site URLs lose that visual table unless they switch browsers (such as Firefox or Safari, which retain XSLT for the time being) or use a dedicated HTML sitemap.

    It has been revealed that because search crawlers ignore XSLT, you don’t need to rush to make emergency fixes. Choose from the steps below based on your role and client needs:.

    Note: This is only a visual change. Chrome 158’s removal of XSLT support only affects how sitemaps render in human browsers. Search engine crawlers process raw XML directly and are completely unaffected.

    In a recent development, organic performance, indexing, and rankings remain safe. WordPress 7.2 will remove the stylesheet reference and, with it, the Chrome warnings, leaving core sitemaps as plain XML. Yoast SEO 28.9 will restore a styled view using CSS, while Rank Math and AIOSEO have not confirmed a change.

    Federal funding for public media is coming back, one way or another. But is it time for a deeper rethink?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    According to recent reports, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    According to recent reports, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Congressional Democrats will have to determine whether they want to revive the old system Donald Trump defunded or build something more attuned to today’s media ecosystem.

    It was 318 days ago that the Corporation for Public Broadcasting — the primary funder of public media in the United States since 1967 — officially ceased to be, the victim of Republican budget cuts and years of attacks from Donald Trump. CPB is not “on pause” or “in hibernation” — it’s dead. As its final CEO Patricia Harrison put it: “CPB’s final act would be to protect the integrity of the public media system and democratic values by dissolving, rather than allowing the organization to remain defunded and vulnerable to additional attacks.”.

    In a recent development, you may have heard, however, that we had some elections in the U.S. recently, and the Republicans who defunded NPR and PBS will no longer control the House of Representatives or Senate as of January 3. In their place will be Congressional Democrats much more favorable to public media. So it seems quite likely that the federal government’s next budget will re-fund it rather than de-fund it.

    But with CPB officially no more, Democrats will have a rare opportunity to rethink the system from scratch instead of just prescribing minor tweaks to funding levels. The media environment of 2027 will, it goes without saying, be radically different from 1967’s. Over-the-air broadcasting is no longer America’s dominant medium. The immensely profitable newspapers that were the bedrock of news back then are shells of their former selves. And what was once a highly localized information ecosystem has been thoroughly nationalized and globalized, with access to news increasingly determined by a few large tech platforms. Democrats could just revive the old LBJ-era model — but should they instead build something upcoming?

    These questions will dominate the next year of discourse around public media, and interested parties are already laying out plans. This morning, the Roosevelt Institute released a new white paper titled “Creating a New U.S. Public Media System: Normative Arguments and Policy Options.” Written by Penn professor (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Victor Pickard, it argues for a thorough reinvention:.

    Taken together, the 2025 federal defunding of American public media, the ongoing collapse of local journalism, growing media oligarchy, a multitude of social harms arising from unregulated platforms and AI technologies, and other political and economic challenges to our media and democracy demonstrate the need for robust public media systems. Fundamental flaws — especially its funding mechanisms — are baked into the historical U.S. public media model, and they must be structurally addressed. The current crisis presents a unique opportunity to create an entirely new kind of public media system based on a local “Public Media Center” model. Pickard lays out three core ideas: de-privatization, democratization, and localization. De-privatization means more thoroughly removing “public” media from the interests of the private sector. No more sponsorship messages from Monsanto or ExxonMobil, no more need to pitch corporations or beg listeners for the funds needed to pay reporters. Pickard wants the public media system to be entirely publicly funded, to the tune of roughly $30 billion a year. That would be a massive increase — almost 60×! — from the pre-Trump level of federal funding, which was around $500 million a year. Even if you include all non-federal sources of revenue, $30 billion would still represent a public media system 8 to 10 times larger than what exists today. (Pickard dreams major!) RELATED ARTICLEDo countries with better-funded public media also have healthier democracies? Of course they doJoshua BentonJanuary 24, 2022But the fact that $30 billion sounds enormous is mostly about how small U.S. public media has always been compared to its international peers. Before defunding, the U.S. spent roughly $3 per person per year on public media. Compare that to countries like Norway ($110), Finland ($101), Denmark ($93), the U.K. ($81), France ($76), Czechia ($60), Japan ($53), Australia ($36), and Canada ($27). If Pickard got his $30 billion wish, U.S. public media funding would sit at about $88 per capita — BBC territory, roughly speaking. But even getting to the level of Canada or Australia would mean a huge increase. By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades: Endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence. Toward this aim, a public media system should not be public in name only but actually owned and controlled by local communities. To encourage trust and community investment, this collective ownership and governance must translate to public participation in all stages of media production and dissemination. In fact, public media institutions are often cross-ideological islands of trust in an otherwise dismal landscape. This trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

    Pickard lays out three core ideas: de-privatization, democratization, and localization.

    Industry observers note that de-privatization means more thoroughly removing “public” media from the interests of the private sector. No more sponsorship messages from Monsanto or ExxonMobil, no more need to pitch corporations or beg listeners for the funds needed to pay reporters.

    By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades:.

    Endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

    Recent findings suggest that and for Pickard, localization is a logical response to the de-localization of media that the internet hath wrought. Many public radio and TV stations primarily serve as distributors of national content, in large part because funding is nowhere near robust enough to create enough local programming to fill each day. And no matter how much you like Ken Burns or All Things Considered, sending the same programming nationwide can limit the range of a community’s residents who might be interested. He advocates pushing more control away from a federal-level entity like CPB and toward states, counties, and cities via block grants.

    Pickard describes the nodes of this system as Public Media Centers: “multimedia hubs that are federally guaranteed but locally owned and democratically governed,” which “would provide journalism, broadcasting, digital media, and other information services based on community needs.”11“Public Media Centers” is also what Pickard called them in one of his first public articulations of the idea, in his 2021 prediction here at Nieman Lab. Some might be housed in existing public radio or TV stations, others in post offices or libraries. And individual communities would be able to determine which media formats work best for them, rather than being locked into the expensive broadcast infrastructure required to reach audiences in 1967.

    I am obliged to note that there are a huge number of barriers to Pickard’s vision becoming reality. Most obviously: $30 billion a year is a lot of money. That’s around the annual budget of the federal school lunch program ($32 billion), FEMA ($32 billion), or NASA ($25 billion). Secondly, the commercial media industry would not sit quietly while the federal government funds an enormous upcoming rival that doesn’t need to sell ads or subscriptions. (For context, the entire U.S. newspaper industry pulls in around $20 billion a year in revenue.) And American suspicion of “state-funded media” goes deep enough that I can’t imagine Democrats looking to retake the White House in 2028 deciding this is the hill to die on.

    But the upcoming Congress is still weeks away from convening, and the next federal fiscal year starts more than 10 months from now. This is the season for major dreams, for expanding the edges of the Overton window, and in that sense, Pickard’s ideas should give newly empowered policymakers a lot to think about.

    More than a year ago, NHPR reporter Todd Bookman started asking questions about “an irregular personnel maneuver” involving the chief justice of Fresh Hampshire’s Supreme Court. Bookman’s reporting ultimately became “Exhibit A” in the ethics probe that led to the justice’s resignation in September.

    The bombshell resignation news was NHPR’s biggest story in September — and of 2026 to date. The story helped push NHPR up several spots in our regular ranking of public radio websites. NHPR saw visits rise 22% that month, according to Similarweb visit figures compiled by Nieman Lab.

    RELATED ARTICLECollaborations and primary elections boosted traffic to public media sites this quarterNeel DhaneshaJuly 29, 2026At the very top of the list, not much moved. The Chicago Sun-Times, owned by Chicago Public Media, held onto the top spot, followed by Gothamist (from WNYC) and Minnesota Public Radio. As Nieman Lab senior writer Joshua Benton wrote when introducing the rankings, which we’ve also done for local newspapers and local nonprofit news sites, not all markets are created equal. Public radio stations serving major metropolitan areas with lots of college graduates have a bigger potential audience than stations serving smaller communities and areas with fewer resources. And, of course, Similarweb provides an estimate; internal metrics may differ. Still, the rankings are a valuable window into some industry-wide trends, and often an opportunity to highlight local news organizations punching above their weight.

    Like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. Newly introduced Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, remarked NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier. “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said. “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added. On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.” BREAKING: Fearless reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026 WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September. Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped. “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.” “Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also important to take advantage when it delivers,” she added. Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said. Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.” The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15. According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary. “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.” And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.” “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.” If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers. “The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.” Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah. Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total owners are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill. All in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case. “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%. Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit. “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.” Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.     Like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. New Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, remarked NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier.

    “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott stated.

    “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added.

    On the audience side, McDermott noted that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.”.

    BREAKING: Fearless reporting by Newly introduced Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp.

    — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026.

    It has been revealed that WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September.

    Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, noted organic search traffic and Google Discover helped.

    “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.”.

    Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.”.

    Industry observers note that the Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15.

    According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary.

    Sources indicate that “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she noted. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.”.

    And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.”.

    In a recent development, “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.”.

    Recent findings suggest that if you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers.

Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds.     “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill remarked. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%.

    Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit.

    Recent findings suggest that “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.”.

    #8160. Google’s Next Upgrade Won’t Touch The Index, And Nobody Will Announce It via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1737 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Google’s Next Upgrade Won’t Touch The Index, And Nobody Will Announce It via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the viral version of Google’s latest research post notes the model makes itself smarter, and the post itself says something more useful to anyone whose job depends on what Google remembers about their firm.
    • In March I argued that the training data cutoff had become a ranking factor, because content on the two sides of the cutoff lives in different systems with different confidence behavior, and I suggested timing key claims to land before major training runs.
    • The post describes a two-phase lifecycle.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the viral version of Google’s latest research post notes the model makes itself smarter, and the post itself says something more useful to anyone whose job depends on what Google remembers about their firm. On Oct. 27, Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni of Google Research published the sleep framework, a method that gives a language model a scheduled offline phase in which it moves what it picked up during use into its long-term weights, then rehearses on data it generates for itself. The viral framing is wrong in a specific way: the post states that the method operates within a fixed architecture under human-defined training rules, so nothing is modifying itself without supervision. What that framing misses is the part that matters here. If this design ships, the knowledge inside Google’s models stops being frozen at a cutoff and starts updating on a cycle that nobody outside Google will see.

    In March I argued that the training data cutoff had become a ranking factor, because content on the two sides of the cutoff lives in different systems with different confidence behavior, and I suggested timing key claims to land before major training runs. That advice assumed the cutoff was a wall with a date on it. This paper describes a wall that moves on its own schedule, without a date, and the right way to read it is as the next form of the Google revision: one that changes what the model believes rather than how the index is ranked, and that arrives with no announcement because there is no event to announce.

    The post describes a two-phase lifecycle. During a wake phase, the model takes input and holds latest information in fast, short-term memory components, which is roughly what context does today. During a sleep phase, it stops taking input and runs two stages. The first is consolidation. The model unlocks new, previously dormant low-rank experts inside a mixture-of-experts layout, assigns them to slower-updating memory blocks, and distills the short-term traces into them through a process the authors call knowledge seeding, which in plain terms means the new facts get their own fresh parameters rather than being written over old ones. Then the temporary parameters are reset so the capacity can be reused. The second stage is what the authors call dreaming. The model generates synthetic samples by randomly routing across its experts so that knowledge from different domains mixes, filters those samples with a gradient-based selection method, and fine-tunes on the ones that survive.

    According to recent reports, the reported results come from four settings: sequential translation into languages the model had never seen, where standard fine-tuning and in-context approaches forgot earlier languages, and the sleep model held a near-zero performance drop; recall on a long-context benchmark out to ten million tokens; factual knowledge incorporation from document passages, where the sleep model beat supervised fine-tuning and a prior self-editing method; and math reasoning on an open 8-billion-parameter base model. The underlying paper has been on arXiv since June and on OpenReview since September 2025, so the blog post is Google deciding to say this out loud, not Google discovering it.

    This is not a one-off. The same authors published Nested Learning in November 2025 with the Hope architecture and the idea of a continuum memory system, a chain of memory blocks that patch at different frequencies, with the fast blocks holding short-term information and the slow blocks holding durable knowledge. The sleep framework is what you build once you have blocks that update at different rates: a schedule for moving information from the fast ones to the slow ones. Titans came before Hope, Hope came before sleep, and the arc now runs about two years. The autoregressive ranking paper I covered in September closed a five-year arc on how results get ordered. This one is younger and just as deliberate.

    It has been revealed that it is research, not a product. The post makes no statement about deployment, timelines, or which Google models might use it. The experiments run on open Qwen models at 1.7 and 8 billion parameters, not on Gemini. No compute cost is reported for a sleep cycle, and no one outside the team has replicated the results. In the experiments, the upcoming facts arrive as documents, not as user conversations or crawled web pages, so anyone claiming the model learns from your chats is extrapolating past the paper.

    Recent findings suggest that those caveats are real and they do not change things. Google publishes research arcs and then ships pieces of them, and that pattern has held often enough that the practitioner question is not whether this exact method lands but what the design tells you about the direction. The direction is a model whose long-term memory is rewritten on a cycle.

    Recent findings suggest that anyone who has done this work for more than a few years lived through the first version of this shift. Google states it updates Search thousands of times a year and shares only the ones it considers notable, and in a 2022 interview Danny Sullivan put the previous year’s experiments and quality tests above 800,000. The named core updates are the handful that get a dashboard entry. Everything else lands continuously and silently, and the industry adapted by building a diagnostic ritual around the named few: traffic moves, you check the date against the update trackers, and attribution follows.

    Sources indicate that retrieval already took the same path for freshness. AI Overviews and grounded answers pull new pages daily with nothing confirmed, so a claim that silence is new would be wrong. What the sleep framework changes is which layer goes silent. Retrieval changes what the model can look up. Consolidation changes what the model believes without looking anything up. Those are different things for a brand. A retrieved fact is cited, hedged, and replaceable the next time the page is fetched. A consolidated fact is spoken with the confidence of something the model knows, and the March piece covered why that confidence difference shapes how a brand appears in an answer.

    So the shape practitioners already know, revealed core updates on the outside and unannounced tweaks between them, gets a second copy one layer down: announced model versions on the outside, unannounced consolidation accumulating between them. The ranking stack does not go away and this does not replace it. It sits on top of it, in the model that writes the answer.

    It has been revealed that the detail in the post I keep returning to is that consolidation is selective. The authors say the model is not asked to copy every detail from its short-term traces into its parameters, and the dreaming stage scores its own samples with a gradient-based filter before anything is trained on. That is a ranking function. It decides which facts the model will carry forward as durable knowledge and which it will let expire with the temporary parameters. Being seen during wake is not being learned. Being learned is what being indexed used to mean, and the thing deciding it is a loss calculation nobody outside Google can inspect.

    Three consequences follow, and the first two are my inference from the design rather than claims the paper makes.

    In a recent development, first, the filter will favor facts that are consistent across sources. A gradient-based selection method keeps samples that reduce error broadly, and a fact that agrees with everything else the model has seen reduces error more reliably than one that contradicts a competitor’s page, a stale directory listing, or your own older content. Conflicting versions of your company are no longer only a conflation risk at retrieval time, which I covered when German courts started holding the platform responsible for false answers, but a consolidation risk, because the version that gets learned is the one that fits best, not the one you prefer.

    Second, dreaming means the model rehearses on data you never published. The synthetic samples are generated by mixing experts across domains, so the model’s representation of a organization can shift through rehearsal with no latest input from anyone. No competitor moved, no page changed, no patch ran, and the answer about you is different anyway. This is a candidate mechanism for a question I have been asked repeatedly this year, which is why an answer changed when nothing observable changed.

    Third, and this one sits in the paper’s design directly, there is a window. Between a fact entering the fast memory and the next consolidation, a correction is cheap because nothing durable has been written yet. After consolidation, fixing a false fact is no longer a matter of updating a page and waiting for a recrawl. It is unlearning, and removing one specific fact from a model’s weights without damaging the rest remains an open research problem. The term I would use is the consolidation window, the period in which a wrong fact can still be caught before the model commits it, and the uncomfortable property of the window is that its length and timing are unknown to you.

    Recent findings suggest that if no Google model announcement within roughly 18 months references periodic updates between releases, continual learning in production, or anything resembling a consolidation cycle, this stays a research direction, and the cutoff stays a wall. If the compute cost of a sleep cycle turns out to be comparable to a training run, the economics kill the cadence idea even if the method works. And if Google chooses to publish consolidation events the way it publishes core updates, the silence argument fails and the diagnostic ritual survives with a new row on the dashboard. I think the third is the least likely of the three, because Google has never published its unnamed changes and has stated plainly that it does not intend to.

    The useful response is to stop building process around an event that may stop existing.

    The cutoff-aware calendaring I suggested in March still holds for the next major training run, because those will keep happening. What changes is the half-life of the word parametric. The safest assumption is that what the model knows about you is being revised on a schedule you cannot see, by a filter you cannot inspect, and that the only observable is the answer itself.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers.
    • In a recent development, we're looking for an Engineering Manager to lead the Realtime team at Supabase.
    • It has been revealed that realtime is a globally distributed Elixir cluster built on Phoenix.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    In a recent development, we're looking for an Engineering Manager to lead the Realtime team at Supabase. Realtime lets developers send low-latency messages between clients, track and synchronize user state, and listen to database changes. Those three features are Broadcast, Presence and Postgres Changes. Broadcast also sends from the database and over HTTP, and clients can replay recent messages.

    It has been revealed that realtime is a globally distributed Elixir cluster built on Phoenix. The team balances low latency, fair limits between projects, and the cost of running the service. Customers expect connections to stay up, so reliability matters as much as fresh features.

    The Engineering Manager is a people, delivery and technical role. We don't expect you to write production code, but you you will lead a team of experienced engineers. We do expect you to join design discussions and help set the bar for engineering quality, testing and operations.

    Build a healthy, high-trust team culture in a remote-first, globally distributed environment.

    Run 1:1s, performance management, career development, and onboarding for your direct reports.

    Handle people admin (leave, time off, etc.) for your team.

    Own the hiring plan for your team and act as Hiring Manager. First round of interviewer for all roles on the team.

    Partner with Talent Acquisition to source, interview, and close strong candidates.

    Contribute to headcount planning, org design, and the evolution of engineering leadership at Supabase.

    Own the team's roadmap and project management (Linear), driving accountability and clear milestones.

    In a recent development, manage workflow intake and Slack triage. These are the team’s primary inboxes for cross-team requests. You decide what gets routed where, prioritized, or pushed back on.

    Own the team's weekly updates and keep stakeholders aligned without creating overhead.

    Organize effort against support tickets and maintain the team's SLO.

    Surface risks, dependencies, and tradeoffs early and clearly to leadership.

    According to recent reports, train as an Incident Commander. Drive coordination, resolution, and post-incident follow-up.

    Lead blameless post-incident reviews.

    Have 5+ years of engineering background, with enough depth to be credible with engineers building complex systems.

    Have 3+ years managing remote engineering teams.

    Have managed a team that built and ran a low-latency, high-connection service. Examples are WebSockets, pub/sub, messaging, presence or streaming systems.

    Have strong technical credibility in distributed systems. We look for clustering, rate limiting, backpressure and capacity planning.

    Have led a team through production incidents on a customer-facing service. You ran the follow-up work and kept the review blameless.

    Understand what developers need from a real-time API or SDK, and have shipped one to customers outside your firm.

    Have experience with Elixir, Erlang or BEAM (not required but a plus).

    Have experience with Postgres logical replication and Row Level Security (not required but a plus).

    Have managed remote, globally distributed teams that work asynchronously across disparate time zones.

    It has been revealed that are technical enough to be credible with strong engineers, but genuinely passionate about people management. This is the work you want to do, not a track you're settling for.

    Build psychological safety and a feedback culture. You give feedback often and in the moment, ask for it back, and create space for the team to do the same.

    It has been revealed that operate as a multiplier. You help individuals achieve more than they could alone, and you don't need to be the best technical voice in the room.

    In a recent development, coach rather than direct. You remove blockers, connect people to context, and trust your engineers to own how the work gets done.

    Have a real track record of performance management and can speak to specific examples of difficult conversations.

    Are comfortable with ambiguity and can build structure where there isn't much.

    It has been revealed that communicate clearly and write well. You default to async and written, set context early, and surface risks early.

    According to recent reports, are collaborative, low-ego and adaptable. You thrive with high-autonomy senior engineers who don't need you to be the smartest person in the room.

    It has been revealed that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    According to recent reports, every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are vital to us.

    Once a year, the entire organization gathers in a fresh city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    Industry observers note that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    #8154. 21 Alternative Search Engines You Can Use Instead of Google via @sejournal, @lorenbaker

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3901 w)

    21 Alternative Search Engines You Can Use Instead of Google via @sejournal, @lorenbaker

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, for many people, searching the web means opening Google.
    • It has been revealed that but the search engine you use out of habit is not always the best tool for the job.
    • Industry observers note that that is where alternatives earn their place.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, for many people, searching the web means opening Google. It’s a familiar place to research a purchase, check a fact, or catch up on the news and that reach reveals in the numbers with Google accounting for 91.04% of worldwide search engine referrals according to Statcounter in October 2026.

    It has been revealed that but the search engine you use out of habit is not always the best tool for the job. Think about the last time you needed an image you could reuse, a webpage that had disappeared, or a more private way to search. Those are different problems, and a single search box is not always the easiest way to solve them.

    Industry observers note that that is where alternatives earn their place. Some give you more control over privacy and rankings, whilst others bring together sources in a conversation, search a specialist collection, or help you explore the content people use in another country. For marketers, those differences also explain why visibility beyond Google involves more than submitting a website to another engine.

    Recent findings suggest that you don’t have to give up Google to find out what you might be missing. We collated 21 alternative search engines and tools worth trying, whether you’re looking for a better answer or a newly introduced way for customers to find your business.

    In a recent development, about the Usage Figures: Entries are ordered within each section by estimated monthly visits to the named website or subdomain. The October 2026 figures are not unique consumers, search queries, or app activity. Statcounter percentages shown separately measure search referral share, not visits.

    Recent findings suggest that estimated Monthly Web Visits: 6 billion to chatgpt.com, October 2026. This covers the ChatGPT website, not Search alone.

    According to recent reports, chatGPT is useful when your question needs a conversation rather than a fresh set of keywords each time. You can ask it to compare two approaches, explain an unfamiliar term, and then look for recent evidence without starting over. Its advantage is keeping the context of that investigation together.

    Industry observers note that openAI’s search documentation claims it can retrieve current web information and link to sources. Search is available on free and paid intends, including for people who are not signed in, although usage limits apply. ChatGPT may search automatically, or you can select Search from its tools.

    In a recent development, use it to work through a question, then open the citations to check the answer. It can misread a source or miss a qualification, and its use of other search providers means it is not simply a separate, independent web index.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 88.3 million to perplexity.ai, October 2026.

    Perplexity puts source-backed answers at the center of the search experience. Its research-oriented approach is useful when you want an overview of a subject and a trail of sources to investigate, rather than opening a long list of results before finding the main points.

    Its Pro Search process can conduct multiple searches and bring findings together, with follow-up questions keeping the research in context. Depending on your initiative, you can narrow the work to areas such as academic or financial sources. Access and limits vary by tier.

    Recent findings suggest that the benefit is a faster route into a topic, not a substitute for reading the evidence. Check that each citation supports the statement beside it because AI answers can still contain hallucinations even when links are present.

    Sources indicate that why SEO Experts Should Care: Perplexity can be useful even if it sends less traffic than Google. In his post on why marketers should care about Perplexity, Dennis Goedegebuure argues that it is a low-cost test bench for AI search. Try the research questions your customers ask, inspect which pages get cited, and check how your brand and recently updated facts appear. For B2B marketers, that means testing visibility during product research, rather than judging the opportunity solely by overall visit totals.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 3.7 billion to bing.com, October 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that bing is a full-service alternative for everyday web, image, video, and news searches. One concrete reason to try it is Visual Search: when you have a picture of a product, plant, or object but do not know its name, you can start with the image instead of guessing keywords.

    Microsoft’s visual search tools can find related images and shopping options, identify objects, and extract or translate text from a picture. Conventional results remain available alongside AI-assisted tools, so an answer does not have to be the end of your search.

    Search Engine Journal covered Bing’s search updates in December 2024, including work on faster, more precise results. Try the same image or video query on Bing and Google to see which makes the next step easier for you; that is more useful than assuming one wins every search.

    Where available, Bing’s Copilot Search adds AI-generated summaries with source citations and suggested follow-up topics, so you can explore a question without starting from scratch.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 751 million to search.yahoo.com, October 2026.

    It has been revealed that search Engine Referral Share: 2.54% in the U.S., October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    Yahoo Search makes the most sense if you already use Yahoo for news, finance, or other daily information. Its value is the connection between search and that wider content ecosystem, rather than a completely different index of the web.

    In a recent development, yahoo introduced Scout in January 2026 as an AI answer engine combining open-web information with Yahoo content and data. The U.S. beta launch named Anthropic’s Claude and Microsoft’s Bing grounding API as parts of the system.

    According to recent reports, that gives Yahoo users a way to move from a headline or financial topic into a sourced explanation. You can still browse traditional search results, and you should follow Scout’s source links when an answer matters. The launch’s audience figures cover Yahoo’s broader services, not people using Scout alone.

    At Search Engine Journal, Yahoo accounts for about 0.2% of our traffic. It’s a small share, but it still brings a few thousand visits in a month and for a different business, even that smaller stream of visitors could include a potential customer or lead to a sale.

    Recent findings suggest that estimated Monthly Web Visits: 1.7 billion to baidu.com, October 2026. This includes non-search activity on the named website.

    According to recent reports, search Engine Referral Share: 49% in China, October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    Baidu matters when your research or marketing is aimed at Chinese-language audiences. Its value is not simply in translating an English query, but it offers a view of Chinese-language search and a connected set of local content services.

    Industry observers note that alongside web results, its homepage links to maps, images, video, the Baike encyclopedia, Zhidao questions and answers, and Wenku documents. Those services give you distinct places to investigate how a topic, product, or brand is described. Use the terminology that local sources use rather than assuming an English search will surface the same material.

    In a recent development, for marketers, the search referral share is a reason to investigate Baidu separately, not proof that it will send a particular site traffic. Distinguish content hosted inside Baidu’s services from results linking to external publishers, and assess the original source.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 1.5 billion to naver.com, October 2026. This includes non-search activity on the named website.

    Search Engine Referral Share: 42.25% in South Korea, October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    According to recent reports, naver is useful for Korean-language research because its search experience brings together more than external webpages. Naver’s search overview describes results across news, maps, cafés, blogs, images, video, and other categories.

    That mix gives you a route into local experiences and community content as well as conventional reporting. Its community services include Naver Blog, interest-based Café communities, and Knowledge iN questions and answers. If you are researching a Korean product or audience, those are different sources to explore from an English-language web-results page.

    For website owners, Naver Search Advisor is the official starting point for webmaster tools. Keep visits to an external website separate from engagement with a blog or other content hosted inside Naver.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 162.2 million to yandex.com, October 2026. This covers the international website, not total use across all Yandex domains.

    Search Engine Referral Share: 70.22% in Russia, October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    Sources indicate that yandex is worth checking when you need Russian-language sources or are researching visibility in Russia. Its large share of measured referrals there gives it a different role from a small global alternative – it is an important regional search environment in its own right.

    Recent findings suggest that use it to compare which local publishers and pages appear for the terminology your audience actually uses. Its international homepage also presents an AI search option, but the practical reason to investigate it is the regional results and audience context, not simply another chatbot interface.

    SEJ’s Yandex guide provides background for marketers. The 2023 data leak is a separate historical event, not a verified description of today’s ranking system. The search referral share above describes referrals, not the percentage of Russian people using Yandex.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 16.5 million to sogou.com, October 2026.

    Sogou offers another route into Chinese-language information, with a more specific reason to try it rather than simply comparing general web results – its WeChat search is a destination for discovering public accounts and articles from that ecosystem.

    According to recent reports, that is useful when the material you need was published as a WeChat article rather than an ordinary standalone webpage. Search in the relevant Chinese terminology and distinguish those public articles from results in Sogou’s general web search.

    According to recent reports, this is not access to private messages or every piece of content in WeChat. As with other platform-specific searches, check the account, publication date, and original article before using a result as evidence.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 698.8 million to search.brave.com, October 2026.

    Brave Search combines an independent web index with tools for changing how results are ranked. It is worth trying if you want both an alternative to Google or Bing’s underlying results and more say over which sources rise to the top.

    Industry observers note that its search help describes Goggles, which apply alternative ranking or filtering rules. Brave also describes domain-level ranking controls and an AI answer experience on its about page. Those controls give you something more specific to experiment with than a different-looking results page.

    In a recent development, SEJ reported Brave’s Bing separation in 2023. You can use Brave Search in another browser, so testing its index does not require adopting Brave’s browser, wallet, VPN, or other products.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 681.9 million to duckduckgo.com, October 2026.

    It has been revealed that duckDuckGo is a straightforward choice if you want everyday search without a personal search-history profile. You can use its search website in your existing browser, so the switch does not require changing your whole browsing setup.

    Recent findings suggest that privacy and index independence are different benefits, however. DuckDuckGo’s source documentation notes traditional links and images largely come from Bing, supplemented by specialist sources, its own crawler, and its own indexes. Choose it for that privacy model, not on the assumption that every result comes from a separate web index.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 57.6 million to startpage.com, October 2026.

    Industry observers note that startpage is for people who want results from major search providers without dealing with those providers directly. It acts as a privacy intermediary, submitting your query on your behalf and returning the results to you.

    Its partner explanation identifies both Google and Microsoft Bing. Startpage claims it does not share personal information with them, and that those providers see Startpage rather than the person making the request.

    According to recent reports, that is the distinction from an independent-index engine: Startpage changes the relationship between you and the search provider, not necessarily the underlying collection of pages. It is worth trying if you like familiar results but want a different privacy arrangement; it is not a way to avoid Google’s infrastructure altogether.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 4.6 million to kagi.com, October 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that its Lenses let you narrow searches to selected websites or categories such as forums, academic sources, or PDFs. Kagi’s source documentation describes its own indexes alongside major and specialist providers, with an emphasis on surfacing independent and noncommercial content. It is not powered solely by its Teclis index.

    As of November 2026, its monthly individual plans include Starter at $5 plus tax for 300 searches and Professional at $10 plus tax for unlimited searches. Annual billing has different terms. If you search heavily and want persistent control over sources, those features are the reason to consider paying.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 219 million to ecosia.org, October 2026.

    It has been revealed that ecosia lets you put the revenue from an everyday habit toward climate work. It says all of its profits go to climate action, with the majority funding tree-planting projects. That is its central reason to exist: changing who benefits financially from search.

    Recent findings suggest that the manufacturer publishes monthly financial reports, so you can look beyond the tree counter to see how money is spent. Its provider documentation lists Bing, Google, and European Search Perspective, or EUSP; the mix depends on factors including region, device, and permissions.

    It has been revealed that this makes Ecosia a funding-model choice, not a promise that every query uses a wholly separate index. If you want to support its mission while keeping familiar web search, it is a low-friction option to try. You can check the provider through the information control beside a result.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 451,800 to karmasearch.org, October 2026.

    In a recent development, KARMA applies the search-funded nonprofit model to animal welfare and biodiversity. Its distinction from a broader climate-focused service is the cause: helping fund organizations working on wildlife, habitats, and animal protection.

    Recent findings suggest that the manufacturer’s explanation says sponsored search links generate revenue for its nonprofit partners. Its site lists partners including Re:wild, Humane World for Animals, and iNaturalist. You can inspect those partnerships to decide whether they match the work you want to support.

    According to recent reports, availability varies by country. During this review, a U.S. capture demonstrated the search homepage, while a visit from another region displayed a notice that KARMA was unavailable there and would redirect searches to Bing. Check local availability before making it your default; a regional restriction does not mean the service has closed.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 155,800 to yep.com, October 2026.

    Yep is an Ahrefs-built alternative with a distinctive audience beyond people typing into a search box: developers who want web results for an AI agent or research application. Ahrefs’ current Yep product page describes a first-party crawler, index, and ranking system, with result excerpts and filters for the information an application retrieves.

    Recent findings suggest that the public search interface captured for this review also returned conventional web results. For an everyday user, that makes it another index to compare; for a developer, the API is the clearer reason to investigate it. The current homepage emphasizes that developer-facing use rather than presenting a Google-like consumer pitch.

    SEJ’s 2022 Yep interview explains the original proposal to share advertising revenue with creators. Although, the current homepage does not establish that those proposed payouts are operating, so they should not be the reason you choose it today.

    Recent findings suggest that estimated Monthly Web Visits: 4.4 billion to x.com, October 2026. This covers platform website activity, not searches or app usage.

    According to recent reports, x.com is useful when the thing you need is a public statement or conversation: what an organization announced, what a named person said, or how a developing event is being discussed. You are searching posts on the platform, not a general index of webpages.

    That direct access to posted statements is its advantage for news monitoring and research. Its advanced search is a further option for signed-in consumers; the public Explore route redirected to a sign-in screen during this review.

    Use posts to locate leads and original statements, not as automatic confirmation of a claim. Check the account, timestamp, and supporting evidence, especially when an old post is circulating as if it describes a newly introduced event.

    Recent findings suggest that estimated Monthly Web Visits: 2.1 billion to linkedin.com, October 2026. This covers platform website activity, not searches or app usage.

    Industry observers note that linkedIn is useful when your search starts with a professional identity, such as a person, employer, role, or job. It can also help you find practitioners discussing a work-related subject, rather than only the publishers ranking for that subject on the open web.

    According to recent reports, the advantage is the professional context. A name alongside an employer and career history gives you a way to distinguish people who share a name and identify a relevant source. Its public people search is one starting point, although fuller profiles and other features can require signing in.

    Treat profiles as self-reported information, not a verified manufacturer directory. Check current roles and dates against the person’s or organization’s own website when those details matter to your research.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 46.4 million to web.archive.org, October 2026.

    The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine answers a question a current search result often cannot: What did this webpage say before it changed or disappeared? It is useful for checking an old product claim, recovering a removed reference, or following the history of a website.

    Enter the URL and inspect the available captures. The advantage is the dated record where you can compare versions rather than relying on a current page to explain its own past. Check the capture date and whether images and other resources were preserved.

    Industry observers note that the Wayback Machine is part of the wider Internet Archive, whose books, recordings, software, and other collections are separate resources. It is not a complete archive of every page, and a captured claim is evidence of what a page remarked then, not proof that the claim was true.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 39.3 million to slideshare.net, October 2026.

    In a recent development, slideShare is worth trying when you want the presentation itself, not another article summarizing the subject. A conference talk, research deck, or business pitch can reveal how someone structures an argument and illustrates the details.

    Sources indicate that the current homepage describes a collection of more than 25 million presentations. Browsing, reading, and uploading do not require a subscription, while features such as downloading presentations are paid benefits. The value is a format-specific collection you can explore for research or presentation inspiration.

    It has been revealed that check the uploader and publication date before relying on a deck’s statistics or recommendations. Being able to view a presentation also does not automatically give you permission to reuse its artwork.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 3.1 million to wolframalpha.com, October 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that wolframAlpha is for questions that need computation rather than a list of pages. If you want to solve an equation, convert units, or work with structured facts, it can calculate an answer from its data and algorithms instead of leaving you to find a suitable calculator elsewhere.

    Its explanation of the service describes dynamic computation over curated knowledge. The mathematics examples show the inputs it understands; other areas include science, dates, and measures.

    That is a different job from comparing recent reporting or finding an opinion. Use it when the result should be computed, and check how it interpreted your units, assumptions, and wording before relying on the output.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 296,200 to openverse.org, October 2026.

    Openverse is the tool to try when finding a usable image or audio track matters more than finding a webpage about one. It focuses on openly licensed and public-domain media, making it useful for an article, presentation, or other creative project.

    According to recent reports, its About page describes a collection of more than 800 million images and audio tracks gathered from multiple repositories, with features such as one-click attribution. That collection size is separate from its website traffic. Its advantage is bringing reuse-oriented discovery into one place, rather than treating every image on the web as equally available to use.

    It has been revealed that openly licensed does not mean free of conditions. Licenses can require attribution or restrict commercial use, and Openverse does not verify every work’s licensing information. Follow through to the original source and confirm the license before using a file.

    The introduction of ChatGPT helped bring conversational interfaces into everyday use. In January 2023, SEJ reported that Google’s founders had responded by returning to discussions about its AI response and then opened access to Bard in March 2023.

    Google rolled out AI Overviews to U.S. users in May 2024 and announced AI Mode in 2025. Those developments explain why many services in this list now combine web results with AI generated answers. The two formats can help with different parts of the same research task.

    Industry observers note that google may be the most familiar option, but the best choice for a particular task can be different. Try a few real queries on two or three services, compare the sources, the ease of finding the original information, and the controls you will actually use.

    According to recent reports, you can keep one engine for everyday searches and use another for a specific job. A calculation, an archived webpage, and a professional profile do not need to start in the same search box.

    Featured Image: Igor Link/Shutterstock.

    According to recent reports, open your browser’s search settings and choose a supported default engine. If the service is not listed, use its official browser setup instructions. You can also visit its website directly without changing your default.

    Start with the task you want to improve. Try Bing for general web search, DuckDuckGo for a search service centered on privacy, Brave Search for another independent index, and ChatGPT or Perplexity for conversational answers. Compare their results on queries you already know well.

    Some do. Startpage identifies Google and Bing as partners. DuckDuckGo largely sources traditional links and images from Bing. Kagi combines its own indexes with several providers. Brave Search builds an independent web index.

    No. DuckDuckGo indicates it is an independent organization. A search provider relationship is different from ownership, and its traditional links and images largely come from Bing.

    Sources indicate that no search tool can guarantee a neutral view of everything online. Index coverage, ranking rules, filters, location, and the query itself affect what appears. Compare independent sources and more than one search engine when the differences matter.

    Business models vary. Some display search advertising, some charge subscriptions, and some combine free and paid services. Read the specific service’s policy because a privacy claim does not mean every product, advertisement, and linked website handles data in the same way.

    Joining Yodo1 Games means more than a job—it means becoming part of a team that lives and breathes games, works with some of the most talented creators in the industry, and is driven by a mission to shape the future of gaming.

    It has been revealed that we love games. We play games. And together, we grow games that last.

    We believe in the future and power of the mobile gaming industry and that everyone deserves an equal opportunity to build a life they love through games—from anywhere in the world.

    We believe you know when and where you do your best work. We are fully remote by design and we WFA: Work From Anywhere. We don’t impose hours or limit time off.

    We are driven by performance and we experiment often. We care about impact, not titles.

    Yodo1 is seeking an experienced, commercially minded Senior Game Scout to identify, evaluate and secure outstanding PC and console publishing opportunities.

    This pivotal role will shape our publishing portfolio, requiring the industry relationships, market knowledge and commercial judgement to recognze exceptional games and distinguish genuine potential from attractive pitches.

    Beyond finding games, the successful candidate will assess their commercial potential, development teams' ability to deliver, and positioning within the competitive landscape.

    It has been revealed that they will own the scouting pipeline, from identifying opportunities and building developer relationships through to evaluation, internal presentation and negotiation. They will also help establish the processes and standards that will underpin our scouting operation as the business grows.

    Industry observers note that focused on impact. You understand the 80/20 rule and focus on activities that matter.

    It has been revealed that performance-driven and growth-oriented. You have an intrinsic will to succeed while unafraid to try, fail, and learn by experimenting with new approaches and testing ideas.

    Industry observers note that cooperative. You help others succeed; you give and receive feedback well.

    Relentlessly curious. You ask questions.

    Recent findings suggest that humble. You ask for help; you are quick to admit and learn from your mistakes.

    In a recent development, SMART. You work and communicate in ways that are Specific, Measurable, Actionable, Relevant, and Time-bound.

    In a recent development, identify and source exceptional PC and console games through industry networks, events, direct relationships and digital channels. Build a strong pipeline of opportunities, developing relationships with independent developers, studios and industry contacts. Focus initially on Steam and Epic Games Store, identifying distinctive games with genuine commercial potential.

    According to recent reports, evaluate creative and commercial potential, assessing gameplay, core loops, depth, replayability, accessibility, audience appeal, differentiation and competitive positioning. Consider potential for streaming, content creation and community engagement, alongside development team capabilities, budgets, schedules, commercial potential and key risks.
