Coordinate due diligence, lead or support negotiations with prospective publishing partners, and maintain developer relationships throughout the process.

    Build the scouting function by establishing processes, evaluation criteria and pipeline management. Monitor market trends and emerging opportunities, report on potential signings, and help recruit and develop the scouting team as the business grows.

    Significant experience in PC/console publishing, scouting, business development or a related commercial role, with an established independent developer and studio network and a track record of identifying and progressing promising games.

    Excellent knowledge of PC and console markets, genres, competitors and player expectations, alongside practical Steam experience, including publishing, launching games and building audiences.

    Strong creative and commercial judgement, with the ability to evaluate gameplay, market potential, development capability and financial viability.

    The confidence to make independent recommendations, challenge assumptions and communicate a compelling commercial rationale, supported by excellent relationship-building, presentation and cross-functional collaboration skills.

    Compensation. We pay based on qualifications, experience, and fit for the role. We provide an allowance to purchase your own device or equipment and offer variable compensation through our annual bonus program.

    Industry observers note that growth. We offer an environment where you will have the trust and freedom to try, fail, learn fast, and make a real impact while accelerating your career, and where anyone with a great idea can pitch it directly to our management team.

    According to recent reports, we’re looking for a Procurement Lead to own the commercial and vendor-management function for Supabase. You’ll run our cloud and SaaS vendor relationships end-to-end (AWS, GCP, Cloudflare, CloudQuery, ClickHouse, and more), leading negotiations and renewals, enforcing procurement governance, and applying our VIA operating model (Visibility, Insights, Actions) to keep vendor spend disciplined and well-governed. You’ll work closely with Finance, Engineering, Legal, and our vendor partners.

    This is a lead role for the Procurement function. The operating model, the source of truth for vendor spend, and the standards are yours to define, against a clear position: this is a FinOps role first, not a pure procurement desk. You'll own the technical and analytical side of vendor management, reporting, efficiency, and the commercial interface across the tech giant, while keeping procurement governance tight. It's ideal for someone fluent across finance and engineering, who thrives in async, fast-moving environments, and wants to build a function from the ground up rather than inherit one.

    Own vendor relationships: run our primary cloud and SaaS vendor relationships end-to-end (AWS, GCP, Cloudflare, CloudQuery, ClickHouse, and more), leading renewals and negotiations alongside Finance and Legal.

    Run procurement governance: enforce our competitive-bid process for incoming requests and manage larger procurement through our managed-procurement partner, keeping oversight and accountability with FinOps.

    According to recent reports, people management: Build a healthy, high-trust team culture in a remote-first, globally distributed environment. Run 1:1s, performance management, career development, and onboarding for your direct report(s).Handle people admin (leave, time off, etc.) for your team.

    Industry observers note that manage team’s delivery and accountability: Own the team's roadmap and project management (Linear), driving accountability and clear milestones. Manage workflow intake and Slack triage. Own the team's weekly updates and keep stakeholders aligned without creating overhead.

    Drive commercial VIA: own spend visibility and unit economics, surface licensing and usage inefficiency before it becomes a surprise, and drive renewals, right-sizing, and tooling consolidation to realized savings.

    Build reporting and governance: vendor and SaaS cost reporting is the unowned gap today and your highest-leverage area in the first year. Build the dashboards and reporting hands-on, partner with our data teams to scale them, and own the governance layer (spend policies, thresholds, accountability).

    Coordinate the cloud efficiency program: keep optimization initiatives visible and tracked from commitment to realized savings, partnering with Engineering without taking over their delivery.

    Have 8+ years in vendor/commercial management, procurement, FinOps, or technical/financial analysis, at a senior, function-owning level.

    Have owned vendor relationships, contract negotiations, and renewals, and treat them as a lever on unit economics.

    Have run procurement governance such as competitive-bid processes, benchmark analysis, approval thresholds, or managed-procurement partners.

    Have high judgment and can hold a position and drive alignment without positional authority.

    Build cost dashboards and reporting hands-on (SQL, BI tools), and are comfortable with vendor and cloud spend data (AWS, GCP, SaaS billing) and licensing/usage analysis.

    Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences.

    Have experience in async or globally distributed teams.

    Are energized by building a function from the ground up and navigating ambiguity.

    Sources indicate that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Sources indicate that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the organization. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Recent findings suggest that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are notable to us.

    It has been revealed that once a year, the entire manufacturer gathers in a upcoming city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Sources indicate that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that at any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government. The right assistance could transform their lives. But today, most never get it.

    In a recent development, atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured American to get life-changing aid. Our mission is to tear down barriers between people in crisis and the aid they deserve. In the last six years, we’ve become the leading platform connecting people with disabilities to government benefits. We also help victims of accidents, misconduct, and violence get compensation from insurance.

    Sources indicate that so far, we’ve helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10 billion in life-changing aid —and earned over 20,000 five-star reviews. And we’re just getting started.

    We've raised more than $100 million from top VC firms like Forerunner, Google Ventures, and True Ventures, and we’re on our way to creating a category defining business assisting Americans in need.

    According to recent reports, each day, thousands of people seek our help getting disability benefits or insurance compensation. They’re intimidated by the process, unsure where to turn, and desperate for good advice.

    Recent findings suggest that as a Legal Assistant at Atticus, your job is to ensure they get and stay on the right path. This job is different from that of a traditional legal assistant. The job mixes responsibilities in any good legal assistant’s comfort zone (build client relationships; support paralegals and attorneys in filing and managing claims) with those unique to being an operator in a fast-growing tech tech giant (help Marketing source clients who’d be great in testimonials, or user test latest tools for Product).

    In a typical week you might do any of the following:.

    Make contact with a client that’s in danger of slipping through the cracks at SSA, and help get their case back on track.

    Work with a client’s team to run down missing paperwork at SSA.

    Take on an inefficient workflow that’s slowing the team down (e.g., processing case updates), scope an improvement, get team buy-in, and execute the improvement.

    Recent findings suggest that this role is a rare opportunity to join a fast-growing Series C startup and do meaningful social impact work.     • According to recent reports, kindred is a members-only home swapping platform that unlocks the ability to live a travel-rich lifestyle through the power of community.
    • Kindred is revolutionizing the “third option” of travel accommodation, compared to short-term rentals and hotels.
    • To support that momentum, Kindred has raised over $150M in capital from some of the most credible investors in Silicon Valley, including Index Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz, Upcoming Enterprise Associates, Bessemer Venture Partners, Caffeinated Capital, Elad Gil, and founders of companies like Opendoor, Figma, ClassPass, and more.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, kindred is a members-only home swapping platform that unlocks the ability to live a travel-rich lifestyle through the power of community. By exchanging primary residences with trusted peers, renters and owners alike can match with Kindred spirits and explore new destinations without breaking the bank.

    Kindred is revolutionizing the “third option” of travel accommodation, compared to short-term rentals and hotels. Since launching in 2022, Kindred has grown to a global community of 300,000 members across 150+ cities and puts home swapping on the map as a radically more affordable, responsible, and connected way to travel.

    To support that momentum, Kindred has raised over $150M in capital from some of the most credible investors in Silicon Valley, including Index Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz, Upcoming Enterprise Associates, Bessemer Venture Partners, Caffeinated Capital, Elad Gil, and founders of companies like Opendoor, Figma, ClassPass, and more.

    Kindred’s co-founders are proven leaders from the early team at Opendoor ($15B+ exit), who have each built and scaled products that today generate $1B+ annual revenue combined.

    We’re looking for the world’s top builders, executors, and believers to help us make travel more meaningful.

    You can learn more about us in Forbes and The Upcoming York Times.

    This is Kindred’s first dedicated public policy hire. You’ll join a three-person legal and policy team (reporting to the General Counsel) and own the execution of Kindred’s public policy and government relations efforts, with a focus on European markets but covering additional markets as necessary.

    The role is primarily focused on proactive advocacy to shape the policy environment for home-swapping. You’ll build relationships with elected officials, regulators, and industry groups. You’ll commission and manage economic impact research. You’ll develop city-level partnerships that normalize home-swapping as a category distinct from other travel categories. You’ll also develop working familiarity with the tax, housing, and accommodation regulations that intersect with Kindred’s model, and help parse how those frameworks apply (or don’t) to credit-based home-swapping. You’ll do all of this initially as a team of one, with outside consultants to support you and a path to building a team as the tech giant grows and the function matures.

    Execute Kindred’s public policy strategy with an emphasis on proactive advocacy.

    Industry observers note that build and maintain relationships with elected officials, regulators, and staff at the local, state/provincial, and national levels. Represent Kindred in meetings, hearings, coalition convenings, and industry events.

    Track proposed housing, short-term rental, tax, and platform regulations that could impact Kindred’s model, identifying where Kindred’s credit-based, non-commercial structure creates meaningful regulatory distinctions. Use AI-assisted tools and other technology to monitor developments across jurisdictions.

    Industry observers note that further develop and evolve Kindred’s core policy narrative and positioning materials. Draft position papers, comment letters, testimony, and advocacy materials.

    In a recent development, propose and negotiate city-level partnerships that promote and normalize home-swapping. Build relationships with housing advocacy organizations, tourism boards, trade associations, and aligned industry coalitions.

    Commission and manage third-party economic analyses on the impact of Kindred’s model, collaborating with internal business teams and outside consulting firms.

    Identify, evaluate, and manage outside consultants cost-effectively (lobbyists, policy advisors, research firms).

    Partner with internal teams to develop externally facing materials and data packages for stakeholder engagements.

    Coordinate with the General Counsel on lobbying compliance, political activity disclosures, and regulatory filings.

    7–10 years of experience in public policy, with at least 3 years at a technology manufacturer or similar fast paced environment.

    Experience building or meaningfully contributing to building a public policy or government relations function, not just operating within an established one.

    Track record of productive relationships with elected officials, regulators, and policy stakeholders.

    Experience managing outside consultants, lobbyists, or policy advisors across multiple jurisdictions.

    Strong written and verbal communication skills, including experience drafting policy position papers, advocacy materials, or regulatory comments.

    Experience with policy matters in Europe, with an interest in policy work in latest jurisdictions.

    Fluency with AI tools and a willingness to integrate them into policy monitoring, research, and content development workflows.

    Willingness to operate as an individual contributor while building the function, with the judgment to know when to engage outside support.

    Experience in or adjacent to the sharing economy, home-sharing, travel, housing, or short-term rental sectors.

    Experience at a growth-stage company (under 500 employees).

    Familiarity with vacation/short-term rental, housing, and land use regulations, as well as related tax regulations.

    Industry observers note that comfort with detailed regulatory analysis: ability to read and interpret statutes, ordinances, and administrative rules, and translate their implications into actionable policy positions. A law degree and legal practice experience is a plus but not required.

    Build something newly introduced: You’ll help define the function and shape how Kindred engages with governments and regulators from the ground up.

    A genuinely different model: Kindred’s credit-based, non-commercial home-swapping model is structurally distinct from existing travel lodging categories, contributing to sustainable tourism objectives.

    Path to leadership: As the manufacturer and function grow, this role offers the opportunity to greater leadership.

    Competitive compensation: Base plus meaningful equity in a growth-stage manufacturer.

    According to recent reports, at Kindred, we know that good things happen when we look out for one another. We offer a thoughtful, human-first benefits package designed to support health, wellbeing, and connection.Our openings may span more than one career level. The base salary offered depends on factors such as experience, transferable skills, business needs, impact, and market data.

    Competitive cash compensation and equity.

    Private health insurance, pension contributions, and enhanced parental leave.

    25 days of annual leave, plus 8 paid bank holidays.

    21 credits per year to stay in Kindred homes.

    £3,200 annual travel stipend to help offset travel-related costs.

    Remote-first and remote-flexible, with a £400 annual budget to meet up with teammates and a yearly organization-paid trip to Kindred HQ in San Francisco.

    Regular team and company offsites to connect, collaborate, and build together.

    A four-week paid sabbatical after five years with Kindred.

    A vibrant, inclusive, and highly skilled team that ferociously protects team chemistry.

    A culture of high standards, feedback, and continual growth.

    Industry observers note that kindred is committed to providing equal opportunities for all applicants and employees. We do not discriminate on the basis of age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, or sexual orientation, as protected by the Equality Act 2010, or on the basis of any other characteristic protected by law. If you need any adjustments during the application or interview process, please let us know.

We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    Kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve. Because this part of our business is growing, we're looking for a Senior Product Marketing Manager, Scaling Creators to own how Kit wins, lands, and expands these businesses through a sales-assisted motion that sits alongside our self-serve product.

    In a recent development, you'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team. When these creators choose Kit and grow on it, they build more valuable businesses, and that's the outcome this role exists for.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role ideal for someone who has added an upmarket sales-led motion to a product-led company before and wants their work measured in win rate and deal size.

    You'll report to Christina Lhi, Head of Marketing, and work alongside two other experienced Product Marketing Managers on Kit's product marketing team. Together, you'll keep the self-serve and sales-assisted stories feeling like one Kit.

    You'll spend a lot of your time with:.

    Our sales leadership, on who we sell to, the deal toolkit, enablement, and win/loss.

    Account Executives and Solutions Consultants, on demo narratives, discovery, and technical and migration proof.

    Product, on packaging, launches, and roadmap input.

    RevOps and analytics, on how accounts get routed to sales, attribution, and pricing decisions.

    Creator Success, on case studies, customer references, and expansion plays.

    Demand gen, content, and events, on campaigns and events for established creators.

    Sources indicate that first Week: Dive into our onboarding curriculum in Notion and learn Kit's product, pricing, and current positioning. Attend Get-To-Know-You (GTKY) meetings with marketing, sales, Solutions Consultants, RevOps, and Creator Success. Get access to our CRM, call recordings, and product analytics, and start listening to recent sales calls. Understand how product marketing presently works at Kit.

    Sources indicate that first Month: Shadow 15+ sales calls and talk with 10 established creators, including recent wins, losses, and churned accounts. Audit the sales content reps use today and how product usage at the moment routes accounts to sales. Set baselines with RevOps for win rate, sales cycle, deal size, and expansion revenue. Share a written point of view with the entire growth team on who our established creator buyer is and the three biggest gaps in how we sell to them. And an action plan on how we can win these creators.

    First Year: Sales runs on messaging and tools you built, pitch with confidence and we drive 2X inbound MQLs from when you started. You’ll own and lead our channel strategy, setting the vision, driving cross-functional alignment, and partnering with Marketing to bring it to life. You'll run a quarterly win/loss program and share what you learn openly, build a clear path for sales leads on our website, and make sure debuts that matter to larger accounts ship with both a self-serve and a sales-assisted version. Your work has a direct impact on helping Kit reach $100,000,000 ARR while protecting the self-serve engine that got us here.

    Segmentation and buyer definition: turning firmographic and product usage data into a clear picture of who to sell to and when.

    Messaging and positioning for a sales-assisted buyer, including competitive differentiation and objection handling.

    Sales enablement that reps actually use: demo narratives, discovery guides, business cases, and battlecards.

    Writing and storytelling that turns product depth into a business case a non-technical buyer can act on.

    Working with CRM, product analytics, and pipeline data to measure funnel conversion, win rate, and deal size.

    Customer and market/competitor research, including win/loss interviews and call analysis.

    Systems thinking: connecting people, processes, data, and tools to identify opportunities and build repeatable solutions across the go-to-market motion.

    Strong AI fluency: knowing when to leverage AI and how to build AI-powered workflows or tools that scale product marketing work, with human judgment and quality checks built in.

    Pricing and packaging input for a latest tier or add-on (nice to have).

    7+ years in B2B SaaS product marketing, including at least 2 years supporting a sales team selling to mid-market and/or larger accounts.

    Added a sales-led motion on top of a product-led one at a high-growth company, and can show what changed before and after with clear metrics.

    Built a deal toolkit and enablement program from little or nothing, and tied it to a sales metric like win rate or deal size.

    Ran a win/loss or customer research program that changed how a team sold or built.

    Ran an expansion or account-based program for an existing customer base (nice to have).

    Worked in email, martech, or the creator economy.

    Industry observers note that you lead without a formal title. You align sales, product, RevOps, and finance on goals, trade-offs, and what success looks like, then keep things moving.

    You advocate for creators in decisions, and you protect the self-serve experience instead of pushing every account toward sales.

    You act with urgency and stay focused on hitting OKRs and owning outcomes.

    According to recent reports, you work in public. You share findings, drafts, and the reasoning behind decisions so others can build on them.

    You connect data to decisions, and you help others get sharper about using it.

    You raise the bar on quality and iterate toward it, and you shape how your team uses AI, from call analysis to keeping battlecards current.

    Experience in only self-serve or only enterprise sales. This role lives in the space between them, and you'll need to understand both.

    In a recent development, treating enablement as a deck handoff. The work includes coaching reps, measuring what gets used, and revising what doesn't land.

    Recent findings suggest that wanting a sales playbook already in place. Much of this motion doesn't exist yet, and you'll be building it as you learn.

    Preferring to be measured on output rather than outcomes. You'll share accountability with Sales for win rate, deal size, and expansion revenue.

    According to recent reports, needing extensive approval before acting. You'll be trusted to make calls on speed versus quality and to explain your reasoning.

    Discomfort with direct, candid feedback, especially from sellers on what's working in live deals.

    According to recent reports, we're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time—so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    It has been revealed that kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we’re hiring at our level 4 ($166,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    Sources indicate that we cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance plans through Aetna.

    Industry observers note that $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Company-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    Industry observers note that winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    A phone screen with our recruiter (30 min).

    Hiring manager interview (45 min).

    #8104. Brands Must Sharpen Their Storytelling For Agentic Commerce

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (853 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adweek ↗ Open Full Page

    Brands Must Sharpen Their Storytelling For Agentic Commerce

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adweek

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When I went from being a Disney entertainment executive to Marriott CMO in 2013, I moved swiftly to bring more storytelling function into a brand environment.
    • The CEO, Arne Sorenson, embraced this move, doing his CNBC interviews from there.
    • It has been revealed that at the time, the marketing industry didn’t have a handle for this structure, and when our team took home a Cannes Gold Lion for the work, the jury assigned it to a upcoming category: Creative Data.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When I went from being a Disney entertainment executive to Marriott CMO in 2013, I moved swiftly to bring more storytelling function into a brand environment. We set up social media hubs around the world, which became a lab for using fresh tech to accelerate company stories.

    The CEO, Arne Sorenson, embraced this move, doing his CNBC interviews from there. Visitors to the headquarters could see how our brand news moved at the speed of culture. Lifting practices and talent from the content business and placing them within a brand was novel to do, and it let social media become visible and repeatable inside a vast organization.

    It has been revealed that at the time, the marketing industry didn’t have a handle for this structure, and when our team took home a Cannes Gold Lion for the work, the jury assigned it to a upcoming category: Creative Data. The years progressed, and social media practices became common and understood.

    In a recent development, agentic commerce will soon impact marketing the way social media has done — both having started with a sense of unknown until hitting critical mass. Plus, storytelling in the age of agentic commerce has a potential topspin when agents, transacting on behalf of customers, gain insight beyond what the brand may have planned.

    Let’s call this Creative Data 2.0, where connected loops help guide internal input and external output.

    According to recent reports, leaders from different departments should meet in one shared group to decide how the company uses newly introduced technology. They’d weigh what the tech can do against the company’s goals, and the kind of presence the brand wants to have. Companies did something similar when social media was new, with several teams working together to figure out how to tell the brand’s story there.

    In this era of AI, marketers influence consumers as well as the agents that act on their behalf. Agentic commerce will eventually convene multiple disciplines to develop a cross-functional playbook in service of coordinated goals. We’ll see transactions optimized because enterprise data presented the product mix to advance the brand story. We’ll see agentic commerce enabling seamless payments and sign on.

    Industry observers note that but brands must be intentional in their strategy and storytelling in order to be known by the agent. In the accelerated pace of AI, the timing and silos of brand storytelling are collapsing, as agents are tracking brand news and “always on” is the norm.

    First, decide what role the brand plays in agentic commerce. From there, it is easier to decide how to assemble the work, influence the agents, and evaluate responses.

    Depending on your brand’s sector or stage of development, these are some of the agentic roles organizations might need.

    Recent findings suggest that advisor: Helps with high level information to navigate options and choices. Beauty brands for instance do this routinely if a favorite product has been reformulated. Brands getting into agentic commerce need to consider being more aggressive updating information whenever there’s a change.

    In a recent development, assistant: Anticipates various use cases and offers personalized options across categories. Think of how retailers organize party planning décor, food, and beverage by occasion. Brands need to think about how to structure information about their entire products in a similar fashion.

    In a recent development, operator: Creates a one stop shop with enough information to empower agents to do the heavy-lifting around shopping and buying. Think of how airlines compile an entire travel itinerary with locations, dates, prices and special activities all the way through to booking the trip.

    It’s important to remember that the agentic advisor is not just content management; the agentic assistant is not just bookmarking the shopping cart; and the agentic operator isn’t just showing promos for related products and services.

    It has been revealed that these agents should act more like a customer’s BFF. They listen to preferences and eventually complete the purchase. And these roles shape the brand story.

    Marketers today emphasize AI for efficiency in creative, performance, and process, but they must now deepen that scope to include agentic commerce.

    Gartner forecasts 20% of commerce will be agentic by 2030, which coincides with predicted 20% adoption of programmable money, or digital funds guided by a framework of rules and safeguards.

    This means the terms of purchase can be automated too. That combination of commercial change is seismic, as agents decide whether your product or service is right for a consumer.

    Who better to navigate customer insight than CMOs, creative leaders with expertise in translating brand value? As storytellers, these skills can creatively power the team’s fresh relationship with agents designed to learn about your brand. As the flurry of AI headlines continues, a clear path exists for marketers and media leaders to bring brand storytelling and agentic commerce closer together.

    In a recent development, karin Timpone is CEO and founder of ClearPrompt, a business strategy advisory with proprietary AI tools that meld human wisdom and technology acceleration. Previously CMO for Marriott and MLB, Karin held senior executive roles at Disney, Yahoo!, Universal Studios, and Seagram.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    Recent findings suggest that kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve. Because this part of our business is growing, we're looking for a Senior Product Marketing Manager, Scaling Creators to own how Kit wins, lands, and expands these businesses through a sales-assisted motion that sits alongside our self-serve product.

    Industry observers note that you'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team. When these creators choose Kit and grow on it, they build more valuable businesses, and that's the outcome this role exists for.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role ideal for someone who has added an upmarket sales-led motion to a product-led company before and wants their work measured in win rate and deal size.

    You'll report to Christina Lhi, Head of Marketing, and work alongside two other experienced Product Marketing Managers on Kit's product marketing team. Together, you'll keep the self-serve and sales-assisted stories feeling like one Kit.

    You'll spend a lot of your time with:.

    Our sales leadership, on who we sell to, the deal toolkit, enablement, and win/loss.

    Account Executives and Solutions Consultants, on demo narratives, discovery, and technical and migration proof.

    Product, on packaging, releases, and roadmap input.

    RevOps and analytics, on how accounts get routed to sales, attribution, and pricing decisions.

    Creator Success, on case studies, customer references, and expansion plays.

    Demand gen, content, and events, on campaigns and events for established creators.

    First Week: Dive into our onboarding curriculum in Notion and learn Kit's product, pricing, and current positioning. Attend Get-To-Know-You (GTKY) meetings with marketing, sales, Solutions Consultants, RevOps, and Creator Success. Get access to our CRM, call recordings, and product analytics, and start listening to recent sales calls. Understand how product marketing at the moment works at Kit.

    It has been revealed that first Month: Shadow 15+ sales calls and talk with 10 established creators, including recent wins, losses, and churned accounts. Audit the sales content reps use today and how product usage presently routes accounts to sales. Set baselines with RevOps for win rate, sales cycle, deal size, and expansion revenue. Share a written point of view with the entire growth team on who our established creator buyer is and the three biggest gaps in how we sell to them. And an action blueprint on how we can win these creators.

    Recent findings suggest that first Year: Sales runs on messaging and tools you built, pitch with confidence and we drive 2X inbound MQLs from when you started. You’ll own and lead our channel strategy, setting the vision, driving cross-functional alignment, and partnering with Marketing to bring it to life. You'll run a quarterly win/loss program and share what you learn openly, build a clear path for sales leads on our website, and make sure launches that matter to larger accounts ship with both a self-serve and a sales-assisted version. Your work has a direct impact on helping Kit reach $100,000,000 ARR while protecting the self-serve engine that got us here.

    Segmentation and buyer definition: turning firmographic and product usage data into a clear picture of who to sell to and when.

    Messaging and positioning for a sales-assisted buyer, including competitive differentiation and objection handling.

    Sales enablement that reps actually use: demo narratives, discovery guides, business cases, and battlecards.

    Writing and storytelling that turns product depth into a business case a non-technical buyer can act on.

    Working with CRM, product analytics, and pipeline data to measure funnel conversion, win rate, and deal size.

    Customer and market/competitor research, including win/loss interviews and call analysis.

    Systems thinking: connecting people, processes, data, and tools to identify opportunities and build repeatable solutions across the go-to-market motion.

    Strong AI fluency: knowing when to leverage AI and how to build AI-powered workflows or tools that scale product marketing work, with human judgment and quality checks built in.

    Pricing and packaging input for a latest tier or add-on (nice to have).

    7+ years in B2B SaaS product marketing, including at least 2 years supporting a sales team selling to mid-market and/or larger accounts.

    Added a sales-led motion on top of a product-led one at a high-growth company, and can show what changed before and after with clear metrics.

    Built a deal toolkit and enablement program from little or nothing, and tied it to a sales metric like win rate or deal size.

    Ran a win/loss or customer research program that changed how a team sold or built.

    Ran an expansion or account-based program for an existing customer base (nice to have).

    Worked in email, martech, or the creator economy.

    Industry observers note that you lead without a formal title. You align sales, product, RevOps, and finance on goals, trade-offs, and what success looks like, then keep things moving.

    You advocate for creators in decisions, and you protect the self-serve experience instead of pushing every account toward sales.

    You act with urgency and stay focused on hitting OKRs and owning outcomes.

    You work in public. You share findings, drafts, and the reasoning behind decisions so others can build on them.

    You connect data to decisions, and you help others get sharper about using it.

    You raise the bar on quality and iterate toward it, and you shape how your team uses AI, from call analysis to keeping battlecards current.

    Experience in only self-serve or only enterprise sales. This role lives in the space between them, and you'll need to understand both.

    Treating enablement as a deck handoff. The work includes coaching reps, measuring what gets used, and revising what doesn't land.

    Wanting a sales playbook already in place. Much of this motion doesn't exist yet, and you'll be building it as you learn.

    In a recent development, preferring to be measured on output rather than outcomes. You'll share accountability with Sales for win rate, deal size, and expansion revenue.

    Needing extensive approval before acting. You'll be trusted to make calls on speed versus quality and to explain your reasoning.

    Discomfort with direct, candid feedback, especially from sellers on what's working in live deals.

    It has been revealed that we're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time—so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    Kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we’re hiring at our level 4 ($166,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    Sources indicate that we cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance plans through Aetna.

    It has been revealed that $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Tech giant-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    Winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    #8093. WTF is a unified media platform?

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2243 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    WTF is a unified media platform?

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2243 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • This article is a WTF explainer, in which we break down media and marketing’s most confusing terms.
    • Editor’s note: These technologies are ill-defined, please share feedback to “editorial@digiday.com” to talk more.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    This article is a WTF explainer, in which we break down media and marketing’s most confusing terms. More from the series →.

    Editor’s note: These technologies are ill-defined, please share feedback to “editorial@digiday.com” to talk more.

    According to recent reports, ad tech has never been short on acronyms. Its latest crop includes: unified advertising platforms (UAPs), unified media platforms (UMPs), and unified buying platforms (UBPs).

    This kind of language has added a latest layer of confusion to the space, and ad executives across adland have been saying, “WTF…?” Digiday is here to help by trying to bring some clarity to the matter.

    A simple way to approach the question is to think of such terms — UAP, UBP and UMP — as overlapping labels for technology that promises to make advertising easier to buy, manage and optimize across an increasingly fragmented media landscape.

    It has been revealed that of course, AI is central to the pitch. Advocates of such technologies maintain that instead of separately operating campaigns across Google, Meta, Amazon and the open web, advertisers could potentially use one system to determine where money goes, then execute those decisions through the relevant platforms.

    Some providers propose bringing buying and selling infrastructure together. Others want to sit above existing systems and coordinate them. This is an crucial distinction to keep in mind, as connective software is not the same as controlling how an advertiser spends its next dollar.

    At its simplest, a UMP coordinates planning, buying, optimization, and measurement across multiple media channels. Its remit could include programmatic display, CTV, retail media, search, social, and direct publisher relationships.

    According to most sources, the idea is not necessarily to replace every existing media trading infrastructure, i.e., demand-side and supply-side platforms, etc., but to make them work together more efficiently.

    That is distinct from the traditional remit of a DSP, many of which have spent years expanding the inventory and formats available through their own buying interfaces. A unified platform, by contrast, promises to operate across buying environments that no single DSP controls.

    Jay Friedman, co-founder of CartographAI, told Digiday that the emerging proposition is about budget fluidity, not simply consolidating DSPs and SSPs. “We define a UMP as a platform that executes buys across all primary digital channels (search, social, programmatic, and direct). This may or may not include agents,” Friedman told Digiday. “Traditionally, this has been the domain of agency order management systems,” he said, noting how several new entrants are hoping to challenge these players.

    Sources indicate that the terms overlap, but they differ in what they promise to unify. The chart below traces that range, from handling an individual transaction to coordinating campaigns across channels and deciding where budgets go.

    Industry observers note that keith Weisberg of Unplugged Collective told Digiday UBPs would initially come to market as a repackaging of existing tools. He stated the deeper shift would come when buyers could bring their data to the places ads run and delegate spending decisions to AI agents.

    In a recent development, “I’d treat that as a net-latest product, not a DSP feature,” he noted. “However, we’re all plugged into DSPs, and even if it’s a new product, it’ll roll out via our current commercial relationships, because that trust (and legal contracting) took years.”.

    In a recent development, ana Milicevic, co-founder of Sparrow Advisers, described the labels as directional distinctions rather than settled product categories. She added, “It’s not all just a collection of black boxes. Then that’s a net newly introduced layer in the stack.” The key distinction is whether a platform merely pushes buttons in existing interfaces or makes independent decisions about where budgets go.

    Ciarán O’Kane, general partner at First Party Capital, was more skeptical about novelty. In wording expressly cleared for attribution, he characterized UMPs and UBPs as “meta DSPs” that act as workflow layers on top of existing systems by plugging into APIs. He also said many emerging players in the space that use this terminology are revisiting approaches the industry has tried before.

    Media-buying teams have long struggled with the fragmentation of conducting ad campaigns using different buying interfaces, datasets, and measurement methods. AI can make the operational work of combining and interpreting those inputs less expensive, but it does not automatically create comparable performance data or independent buying authority.

    “The frustration is very, very old. What’s new now is that AI is letting us operationally skip through some hurdles that were previously insurmountable,” Milicevic told Digiday. Tasks that once demanded a substantial analytics stack and specialist labor can increasingly be assisted by repeatable prompts and automated processes.

    The commercial question is whether cheaper orchestration creates an entirely fresh buyer or simply a more convenient way to operate existing platforms. For advertisers, that distinction determines whether the new technology saves money, reallocates money, or merely adds another vendor to pay.

    It has been revealed that in an Oct. 8 blog post, titled “universal buying platform,” Apostrophe co-founders Brian O’Kelley and Anne Coghlan outlined a broader buying layer intended to connect intent, execution, and measurement across advertising environments, citing the recent launch of Amazon Ads Agent as an example of this trend.

    Their argument is a public proposal, not evidence that a single independent platform already performs every part of the workflow at scale — O’Kelley did not respond to Digiday’s request for comment by press time.

    Other companies are approaching the problem from different directions, with Olyzon — an entity that used the term “agentic orchestration platform” in its recent CTV launch material — serving as one example.

    In a recent development, jules Minvielle, co-founder and CEO of Olyzon, told Digiday the company does not own inventory and uses agents to coordinate buying through existing platforms, with advertiser-controlled approvals. “A DSP is one place where you can buy. Orchestration is all the work around the buy: building the strategy, deciding where each dollar goes, activating across every platform, watching delivery, measuring, and feeding what worked into the next plan,” he wrote in an emailed statement, adding that uneven API access and inconsistent measurement remain substantial obstacles.

    Ravi Patel, co-founder and CEO of SWYM.ai, drew a distinction between a common interface and control over the budget. “It can manage the ‘what’ and the ‘how much.’ It can’t manage the ‘which impression.’ That distinction is the whole story,” he explained, adding that campaign setup and pacing across platforms are already possible through APIs. However, impression-level optimization within the major walled gardens remains in their own systems.

    Industry observers note that lucas Cridland, CEO of Basin Media, questioned whether agents are changing the underlying buying process. “At the moment, many environments are agentically operating in the same supply chain flow. They’re just doing it with agents buying; they’re not radically changing the way the process works. And that’s where the real edge exists.”.

    Industry observers note that not necessarily. Many of the latest propositions depend on DSPs continuing to execute transactions, access inventory, and optimize within their own environments. The change may be who decides which platform gets the advertiser’s budget in the first place.

    Milicevic maintained that “value always accrues to whoever is closest to the decision or outright owns the decision.”.

    Ergo, if DSPs cannot move upstream into genuine cross-channel decision-making, they risk becoming “dumb pipes,” i.e., a commoditized, essential infrastructure whose underlying value is less visible to buyers.

    Incumbent DSPs, however, have established advertiser relationships, bidding technology, data integrations and scale. They could develop their own orchestration capabilities. A new intermediary would need to show that its independence produces better decisions, rather than simply adding another fee, according to several sources consulted for this piece.

    Industry observers note that agencies already coordinate campaigns across channels, negotiate buying arrangements and manage the systems needed to execute them. Friedman, a former long-time agency-lead, argued that unified platforms could challenge agency order-management systems while bringing neglected channels, including creator-led media, into a common workflow.

    Such a scenario would not eliminate strategic planning, creative development, or oversight, but it could change how much manual campaign administration agencies perform, where they develop proprietary expertise, and which services clients are willing to pay for, with AI at the center of many contractual renegotiations between advertisers and media agencies.

    Such a scenario would not eliminate strategic planning, creative development, or oversight, but it could change how much manual campaign administration agencies perform, where they develop proprietary expertise, and which services clients are willing to pay for, with AI at the center of many contractual renegotiations between advertisers and media agencies.

    The biggest obstacle may be the very platforms that independent systems are supposed to coordinate. Google, Meta, and Amazon control their own buying tools, data, and optimization systems. Access through an API does not necessarily provide the granular information or authority required to compare results and independently move budgets.

    It has been revealed that trust is also an concern. A unified interface can display reports from multiple platforms without proving that the outcomes are comparable. Attribution windows, campaign objectives, and self-reported measurement differ across channels, meaning an independent buying layer needs a credible basis for deciding that one dollar is better spent in one environment than another.

    Friedman was skeptical that interoperability would resolve the underlying problems, and highlighted how Google and Meta are unlikely to make their systems interoperable. He further questioned whether agencies could build the context and routing infrastructure needed to translate employees’ instructions into accurate buying decisions, even if every platform supported the Model Context Protocol. “Interoperability won’t solve anything,” he told Digiday.

    Greg MacDonald, founder of Chelsea Strategies, noted addressing media buying’s growing complexity could reduce spending on its mechanics and, over time, potentially improve advertiser outcomes. However, he remained cautious about how far unified platforms could go. “I’m skeptical that the walled gardens will give buyers more control than they have today,” he told Digiday, pointing to persistent difficulties with frequency capping across programmatic formats, let alone disconnected marketplaces.

    Industry observers note that “But you don’t have to solve every problem, and certainly not on day one to be useful,” MacDonald added. He compared the opportunity with programmatic guaranteed buying, which made the insertion-order process more efficient without fundamentally changing direct media buying.

    Meanwhile, Milicevic remarked the more plausible near-term customer may be a multichannel advertiser between the largest global brands and small businesses that largely rely on a single platform. She also stressed the need for independent validation of results, rather than taking each platform’s own reporting at face value.

    It has been revealed that AI agents could help automate campaign setup, inventory discovery, negotiation, execution, and reporting. That makes agentic advertising relevant to the unified-platform debate, but not synonymous with it: automating tasks is different from making accountable, cross-channel budget decisions.

    In a recent development, unplugged Collective maps seven ways AI could change advertising (see graphic below). Per Weisberg, two are central to the unified buying debate: how agents decide where to spend and how they carry out those decisions across platforms.

    It has been revealed that industry initiatives such as AdCP and IAB Tech Lab’s agentic work aim to establish ways for systems to communicate and execute workflows. Technical standards could reduce integration costs, but they cannot by themselves force walled gardens to disclose comparable data or surrender commercial control.

    Seasoned industry observers have seen enough buzz phrases come and go to feel confident enough to make tongue-in-cheek observations when a fresh acronym becomes de rigueur among the industry’s chattering classes.

    “I saw ‘UMP’ and I thought: ad network,” quipped Terence Kawaja, CEO, LUMA Partners, a prominent investment bank in the space, speaking on stage at this year’s Prebid Summit – channeling the industry adage, “everything is an ad network.”.

    Meanwhile, one prominent industry source, who requested anonymity to preserve industry relationships, dismissed the latest acronyms as another serving of “word salad.” However, the barbs, playful or otherwise, raise a palpable industry debate: As AI makes it cheaper to run campaigns across platforms, who gets to decide where the money goes?

    The clearest test is whether advertisers entrust meaningful cross-channel allocation to an independent system — and can demonstrate that the decisions improve outcomes. Smaller-scale automation and campaign management do not, on their own, prove that a newly introduced market category has emerged.

    Milicevic identified three indicators: real advertiser budgets moving under independent allocation, credible measurement outside any single walled garden, and changes in how marketing organizations structure teams. “If it’s truly structural, it’ll show up in the PNL, and if it’s slideware and fluff, then that’ll make its way into award entries and kind of the PR circuit,” she noted.

    For now, the most useful distinction is between controlling the infrastructure through which ads are purchased and controlling the decision about where the money goes. The latter is the more ambitious promise. Whether anyone can deliver it independently, at scale, and at a cost advertisers will accept remains unresolved.

    After 45 years of negotiating, the chairman of Publicis Media Exchange (PMX) U.S., is stepping down from a full-time role this year, although he prepares to continue to consult with the holdco.

    Mediaplus and Publicis clients, including Banco Santander, have paused TikTok spending in wake of investigations into abuse images circulating on the video platform.

    Madison and Wall estimates creator marketing growing at double the pace of the rest of advertising, driven on by creator-led production investments.

    Sources indicate that fingerprint empowers enterprises to detect and stop online fraud with the world’s most accurate device intelligence.     Fingerprint is a globally dispersed, 100% remote firm. We were named on on the 2026 Forbes Best Startup Employers list and ranked #803 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of America’s fastest-growing private companies.

    Fingerprint is looking for a Technical Product Manager (P3) to help turn product strategy into clear, well-executed product delivery. This role is ideal for someone who is building strong product management fundamentals, enjoys working closely with engineering and design, and is energized by keeping product work organized, well-documented, and moving toward release.

    In this role, you will own specific product features or workstreams under the guidance of a Sr Technical Product Manager. You will help translate product intent into clear user stories, jobs-to-be-done, acceptance criteria, release plans, documentation, and operational updates. You will work across Product, Engineering, Design, Product Analytics, Customer Success, Sales, and Product Marketing to ensure product records are accurate, dependencies are visible, stakeholders are informed, and shipped work meets the expected customer and business outcomes.

    This role blends TPM expectations with the Delivery Product Owner operating model: the Sr TPM sets product direction, priorities, success metrics, and major tradeoffs; the TPM helps ensure that direction becomes shippable, well-understood, and well-supported product increments.

    A successful TPM at Fingerprint:.

    At Fingerprint, we believe in pay transparency — it's part of how we operate as a distributed, remote-first team. Salaries are based on function, level, and geographic location, benchmarked against similar stage growth companies.

    Because this role is open across the United States and can be based anywhere our team members work from, the salary range reflects that geographic breadth: $126k - $170k.

    Some example salaries for specific locations are below:.

    Final offer amounts are determined by multiple factors, including the successful candidate's location, experience, and expertise, and may vary from the amounts listed above.

    Due to regulatory and security reasons, there’s a small number of countries where we cannot have Fingerprint teammates based. Additionally, because Fingerprint is an all-remote company and people can join our workforce from almost any country, we do not sponsor visas. Fingerprint teammates need to be authorized to work from their home location.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, join us Dec.
    • Brand spending on creator marketing is set to grow twice as fast as spending on advertising as a whole over the next five years, according to advertising research firm Madison & Wall.
    • The consultancy estimated that creator spending will rise 12% each year until 2030, versus a 6% increase in ad spending each year between 2025 and 2030.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Brand spending on creator marketing is set to grow twice as fast as spending on advertising as a whole over the next five years, according to advertising research firm Madison & Wall.

    The consultancy estimated that creator spending will rise 12% each year until 2030, versus a 6% increase in ad spending each year between 2025 and 2030. In 2026, the researcher estimates that marketers will spend $116 billion on creator activity.

    Driving that growth is ad spend intended to boost or promote creator content to a larger audience — which accounted for 44%, or $52 billion, of global creator marketing spending in 2026 — and brands paying creators to produce advertising assets for use in CTV, display and paid social contexts.

    The latter accounted for 12% of global creator spending in 2026, but will rise 16% each year until the end of the decade, making it the fastest-growing segment of the creator economy. Traditional sponsored posts or ambassador relationships accounted for 28% of creator spending.

    Brands attempting to reach large audiences on social platforms have begun to look to creators not just as a distribution point, but as a source of creative production that can meet the need for a diverse set of creative assets at a lower price point than traditional agency methods.

    Unilever CEO Fernando Fernandez, for example, recently noted that the CPG giant’s social content had to be constantly refreshed to prevent it from going stale. “The lifespan of a video today is four days,” he said during the firm’s recent Capital Markets Day. “Content has to be renovated because after four days you don’t have diminishing levels of return, you have negative marginal return.”.

    Sources indicate that “The reason we see brands engaging with this is just because it’s cheaper,” stated Luke Stillman, managing director at Madison & Wall. “Everybody is trying to squeeze down all those non-working expenses as much as possible.”.

    As creator rosters get larger — Unilever now works with around 500,000 — the need to manage such programs has driven spending on specialist agencies, platforms and talent representation. Spending on creator intermediaries (fees for specialist agencies, platforms, or talent representation) accounted for 8% of global creator spending.

    Industry observers note that stillman said he expected to see spending on that slice grow further in coming years. “Identifying the right creators, contracting with all those creators, managing non-delivery and legal issues and payment issues are really complex, and so there’s plenty of space for ancillary services there,” he said.

    “We’re seeing an increase on budgets year-on-year from our clients,” remarked Andy Ryan, co-founder at social and influencer agency Komodo. Ryan estimated client spending on creator marketing had increased 20%-30% in 2026.

    Olivia Wedderburn, head of influence at Born Social, saw an even bigger jump, estimating that client spending on creator activity had risen 50% compared with last year. “I would anticipate that will only continue to grow quite heavily,” she stated.

    According to recent reports, the U.S. market accounted for 43% of creator spending last year, per Madison & Wall estimates, while the U.K. and Germany are the next-largest, at 5% and 4% respectively. The U.S. will see spending grow 15% this year. India was the fastest growing market, at 20%.

    Madison & Wall’s estimate for asset-led spending covered several related practices: whitelisting, fees for user-generated content, content licensing, and fees for producing creative assets.

    Industry observers note that however brands are commissioning it, creator-led production is on the rise. “More of our brand partners are bringing creators in as the production engine for their paid media, not just their organic social,” said Nicholas Spiro, chief commercial officer at Viral Nation.

    While cost is a major factor, as Stillman noted, agency marketers also believe creator-made work can engage audiences more effectively than an ad made for the same environment by a creative director.

    In a recent development, “Creator-made assets simply connect best with potential customers on a human level,” said Spiro. “They tend to drive performance better than traditional brand creative, and they can be more measurable for certain objectives than organic creator-only content.”.

    While creator marketing was once dominated by apparel and beauty brands, healthcare, automotive and finance advertisers now spend on creator activity too.

    “Where some sectors like fashion and beauty have been on this for a number of years, and therefore they’re already doing a fantastic job at it… some sectors [were] behind and they’re catching up and are now throwing more at it,” noted Ryan.

    “An ad can make a claim. A parent can prove it,” stated Carmen Graham, CMO at Genexa, a youth-targeted healthcare brand.

    Recent findings suggest that “Parent creators can also do what we can’t: show the product in real use, in their home. The messier and less art-directed the medicine cabinet, the more we see ourselves and our customer in the content,” she stated.

    “Our bet is that this commitment to being parent-first will drive the trust this category requires — especially if you’re switching to a new product to support you in the most dire moments of parenthood.”.

    After 45 years of negotiating, the chairman of Publicis Media Exchange (PMX) U.S., is stepping down from a full-time role this year, although he intends to continue to consult with the holdco.

    Mediaplus and Publicis clients, including Banco Santander, have paused TikTok spending in wake of investigations into abuse images circulating on the video platform.

    A fresh crop of companies promise to coordinate advertising budgets across platforms, but can they control buying decisions, or merely add another interface to the existing system?

    Latest Update: Media Briefing: ChatGPT’s upcoming business hub is an early ‘search console moment’ for publishers

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • This Media Briefing covers the latest in media trends for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Thursday at 10 a.m.
    • This week’s Media Briefing looks at what publishers can learn from ChatGPT’s latest AI visibility and click data, how that data fits into their third-party analytics, and what it means for their GEO businesses.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    This Media Briefing covers the latest in media trends for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Thursday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →.

    This week’s Media Briefing looks at what publishers can learn from ChatGPT’s latest AI visibility and click data, how that data fits into their third-party analytics, and what it means for their GEO businesses.

    In a recent development, openAI’s new Business Hub gives brands and publishers access to something they’ve never had before: a first-party view of how they appear in ChatGPT. But legal teams may need to read the fine print before publishers dive in.

    According to recent reports, last week, OpenAI released a ChatGPT Business Hub, a dashboard for businesses that claim and verify their accounts. It offers data on how their sites appear in ChatGPT, including mentions, profile views, website clicks and the topics driving discovery. For publishers, that offers an early view into activity they’ve largely had to estimate with third-party tools or infer from referral traffic.

    “Until now, everything publishers knew about their presence in ChatGPT came from third-party tools running prompts at scale and estimating, or from referral traffic after the fact. This is a very early, very limited Search Console moment for ChatGPT,” said John Shehata, CEO and founder of publisher SEO analytics firm NewzDash.

    Recent findings suggest that publishing execs are mixed on how useful they thought the data would be for their AI visibility and audience development strategies. Of the half dozen large publishers Digiday spoke with for this story, half were in the process of setting up their business accounts.

    It’s early days, but one industry exec, who requested anonymity, remarked legal teams may need to be extra cautious around some of the potential implications of OpenAI’s terms of service.

    Sources indicate that openAI’s terms require businesses to agree not to pursue certain legal claims against the company, including disputes involving content published on their websites before they signed up. That may cause headaches for legal teams at publishers already grappling with how to protect and monetize their content in the AI era, if accessing valuable first-party visibility data comes at the cost of relinquishing certain legal rights — a trade-off that may give some pause before signing up.

    When reached for comment, an OpenAI spokesperson mentioned the terms “were not intended to cover this scenario.”.

    In a recent development, despite those concerns, some publishers see a potential commercial benefit. Two publishing execs said they were interested in using the data to support their GEO offerings. AI attribution and measurement is a major hurdle for those businesses, but they said insights from brands’ first-party data could help publishers assess the performance of branded content campaigns alongside data from third-party tools.

    “These insights potentially provide a really valuable piece of the puzzle that should validate our own success criteria around visibility and citations,” noted Carly Steven, Daily Mail director of SEO and editorial ecommerce.

    Shehata remarked the Business Hub data could help publishers demonstrate the value of their GEO offerings to brands, but cautioned that a publisher’s own visibility metrics don’t prove a brand’s campaign delivered results.

    Recent findings suggest that “With authorized access to a client’s data, [publishers can] finally prove that recommendations move real platform metrics. That closes the measurement loop missing from every GEO pitch. But a publisher’s own citation count is not proof of a client’s GEO return. A brand campaign still needs evidence at the brand level. The commercial opportunity is selling better evidence and better decisions, not citation counts,” he said.

    Another publishing exec was less convinced the data would help their GEO business.

    “Since [the hub] is only [tracking] mentions of the business owner, it isn’t so useful to our needs around influencing AI answers on behalf of partner brands. But we are signing up just so we can see if there’s anything there,” the exec mentioned.

    For example, if a brand pays for a publisher’s GEO offering, that publisher produces sponsored content articles about that brand’s product, and ChatGPT recommends the product with a citation link to the publisher’s sponsored content, the Business Hub wouldn’t report the mention of the product to the publisher, the exec explained. This means publishers will need to continue to use third-party AI visibility tools to measure those citations.

    In a recent development, “At this stage, I see brand mentions in answers akin to billboards. It makes sense for Nike to have a billboard but not [a publisher],” the exec said.

    Lily Ray, vp of SEO strategy and research at performance marketing agency Amsive, pointed out that the Business Hub tracks mentions of a business website, rather than its brand name surfacing in ChatGPT.

    That offers a “limited view” of what is considered a mention in ChatGPT, though Ray expects the measurement to evolve. It also makes click-through rates appear disproportionately high. On the Business Hub dashboard for her SEO consultancy, Ray recorded four clicks from just 25 mentions. While “they’re very small numbers in absolute terms,” Ray said the first-party data gives her another point of comparison against metrics from third-party tools.

    Sources indicate that while the dashboard offers an incomplete picture, Shehata stated publishers can still use its data to establish a baseline and track changes over time. He recommends three steps  publishers take once they get access to their Business Hub data. The first is to use the data to set a baseline for mentions, clicks and discovery topics so that the publisher can evaluate trends over time.

    It has been revealed that the second is to use discovery topics, which are “the most valuable data for audience teams,” to steer editorial experiments, Shehata remarked. These topics show which themes ChatGPT associates with a publisher’s site, where the AI treats the publisher as an authority, and white spaces around topics the publisher wants to own.

    “A travel publisher seeing activity around family travel can strengthen those guides with original reporting and watch whether the numbers move,” Shehata said.

    Publishers should also separate the metrics in the Business Hub dashboard and their outcomes, he added.

    According to recent reports, “A citation is a visibility outcome. A visit is an audience outcome. A subscription or sale is a business outcome. Publishers need to measure those separately,” Shehata said. He suggested publishers compare Business Hub trends against their own analytics, such as ChatGPT referrals, newsletter signups and conversions.

    “If reported visibility grows while referrals stay flat, that raises a hard question about value the dashboard alone won’t answer,” Shehata noted.

    It has been revealed that the Business Hub analytics have a number of limitations that publishers should consider too,  Shehata noted. The data is aggregated, with no prompts, no per-article breakdown, and no competitor benchmarks, he remarked.

    Recent findings suggest that the lack of prompt data means the analytics lack what third-party prompt tracking can provide – and that’s saying something, considering prompt tracking is “deeply flawed,” said Barry Adams, founder of Polemic Digital, an SEO and audience growth consultancy for news publishers. Digiday previously covered the varying methodologies for gathering prompt data by different AI visibility analytics firms, and how much of it relies on synthetic data or panel data, and the efforts publishers have to go through to weed out the GEO solutions from the snake oil.

    According to recent reports, “We don’t know the contexts in which our websites are mentioned, except in the vaguest of terms. That makes it very hard to glean anything useful from these reports,” Adams said. However, Adams pointed out that over time, Google added more useful tracking to its Search Console dashboard, and hoped the Business Hub would also continue to evolve.

    Even though the data is limited compared to what prompt tracking tools offer, the fact that the data is coming from the AI platform itself makes it “extremely valuable,” Ray remarked.

    “It’s another data point for a very convoluted channel,” she said. “It’s not going to replace any of the tools I’m using.”.

    Industry observers note that “This year, we kind of saw more volume. Smaller spends, but new advertisers. It’s too early to tell why that’s happening. If branded content is kind of going in a different direction because of AI and publishers are getting more media spend? I don’t really know. It’s been two wildly different years, this year versus last year.”.

    — John Sills, head of sales, North America at The Guardian.
